The Right to a Body That Is Cared For

A Companion Document to the Constitution

The Philosophical Foundation

Healthcare in the United States is organized around the extraction of profit from human need. The person who is sick needs care. The system that provides care charges for it. The person who cannot pay does not receive the care, or receives it in a form that leaves them with debt that compounds their circumstances, or delays receiving it until the condition is more serious and more expensive to address. This is not a neutral market outcome. It is a political choice: the decision to organize the provision of care around the profit motive rather than around the needs of people who are sick.

The belief that the market is the appropriate mechanism for providing healthcare is presented as economic law rather than political choice. The market price of insulin does not reflect the cost of producing insulin. It reflects the negotiating power of the pharmaceutical company relative to the patient who will die without it. The market price of a hospital stay does not reflect the cost of the care provided. It reflects the billing codes, the insurance contracts, the administrative architecture built around extracting maximum revenue from the encounter between a sick person and the system that can help them. This is a construction. It was built. It can be rebuilt.

The second foundational principle is that the body is not a singular acceptable body. It is plural: it has a history, it carries what it has been given, it presents differently in different people, it responds differently to the same interventions, it has needs that do not fit diagnostic categories built from studies of the median white male patient. The history of medical research is the history of whose body was studied and whose was not, whose symptoms were taken seriously and whose were attributed to hysteria or drug-seeking or non-compliance, whose pain was treated and whose was dismissed. The healthcare system has not been built to receive the full range of human bodies and experiences. This document describes what it would look like if it were.

Universal Healthcare

The Case

Every wealthy democracy except the United States provides universal healthcare coverage to its citizens. The outcomes in those countries, across virtually every measure of population health, life expectancy, infant mortality, chronic disease management, preventable death rates, are better than the outcomes in the United States, at lower per capita cost. The United States spends more on healthcare than any other country in the world and achieves worse outcomes than countries that spend significantly less. This is not a mystery. It is the predictable result of a system organized around profit extraction rather than health outcomes.

The administrative cost of the American healthcare system is itself a substantial fraction of the total cost: the billing departments, the insurance claims processors, the prior authorization systems, the coding and documentation requirements, the collection agencies. A significant portion of every healthcare dollar does not purchase care. It purchases the administration of a system whose complexity is itself a product of the multiple competing financial interests the system serves. Single-payer systems eliminate most of this administrative cost by eliminating the multiple competing payers whose existence generates it.

The argument that universal healthcare requires giving up choice is exactly backwards. The person with comprehensive coverage can choose any provider and receive any indicated care. The person navigating a network of in-network and out-of-network providers, prior authorization requirements, formulary restrictions, and coverage limits has no meaningful choice. They have the bureaucratic appearance of choice within a system designed to deny as much care as possible while collecting as much premium as possible. The choice the current system protects is the choice of the insurance company to deny care. That is not a choice worth protecting.

The Structure

Universal healthcare means every person receives comprehensive coverage for every medically necessary service: primary care, specialty care, mental healthcare, dental care, vision care, prescription drugs, long-term care, reproductive healthcare including abortion, and gender-affirming care. The coverage is not contingent on employment, income, age, citizenship status, or any other characteristic. It is the right established in Article VII of this constitution, enforced by the obligation of the healthcare system to provide it.

The financing is through progressive taxation: the people and institutions with the most resources contribute the most to the system from which everyone benefits. The current system finances healthcare through a combination of premiums, deductibles, copays, employer contributions, and tax revenue that is profoundly regressive: the person who is sickest and poorest pays the highest proportion of their income for the least adequate care. The universal system reverses this: the contribution is proportional to the ability to pay, the benefit is proportional to the need.

Providers are paid fairly and consistently, not through the current system of negotiated rates that produce wildly different payments for the same service depending on who is paying, but through a rate schedule that reflects the actual cost of providing care plus a reasonable return to the provider. The administrative burden on providers, which currently consumes a substantial portion of physician time and contributes significantly to burnout, is dramatically reduced by the elimination of multiple payers with multiple requirements.

Mental Healthcare

Mental healthcare is healthcare. The separation of mental health from physical health in insurance coverage, in delivery systems, in public understanding, and in the allocation of research funding reflects a decision that the suffering of the mind is less real, less urgent, and less deserving of the full resources of the medical system than the suffering of the body. The grief that does not resolve, the anxiety that does not lift, the psychosis that reorganizes reality into something unrecognizable: these are conditions that require care with the same urgency as any other medical condition.

The deinstitutionalization movement of the 1970s was right that the psychiatric hospitals of the era were often sites of abuse and violation rather than care. It was wrong that closing them without building replacement infrastructure would produce better outcomes. The replacement infrastructure was never built. The community mental health centers that were supposed to provide it were never adequately funded. The gap was filled by the criminal legal system, the emergency room, the homeless shelter, and the street. The person with a serious mental illness who cannot access consistent care cycles through these systems indefinitely at enormous human and financial cost to themselves and to the systems that process them without treating them.

Universal mental healthcare means adequate reimbursement for mental health providers that makes the profession financially viable and attracts enough practitioners to meet the need. It means the removal of prior authorization barriers that currently make accessing mental healthcare a bureaucratic obstacle course. It means the investment in community mental health infrastructure that deinstitutionalization assumed would be built. It means the integration of mental healthcare into primary care so that the person who presents to their doctor with depression is not referred away to a system they will never navigate, but treated in the place they already came to for help.

Reproductive Healthcare

Reproductive healthcare is healthcare. The decision to reproduce, to not reproduce, to continue a pregnancy, to end a pregnancy, to use contraception, to seek fertility treatment: these are medical decisions that belong to the individual under the bodily autonomy provision of this constitution. The state has no legitimate interest in compelling any of these decisions. The history of state intervention in reproductive decisions is a history of the control of women's bodies, of the eugenic sterilization of disabled people and people of color, of the criminalization of choices made by people the system has decided should not reproduce or should not stop reproducing.

Universal healthcare coverage for all reproductive services, without restriction based on the political preferences of whoever controls the relevant legislative body at a given moment, is the constitutional requirement. The coverage includes abortion, contraception, fertility treatment, prenatal care, maternal care, and postpartum care. The person who cannot afford to travel to a state where abortion is legal, cannot afford to take time off work, and cannot find childcare for the children they already have is not making a free choice when she carries an unwanted pregnancy to term. She is experiencing compulsion delivered through economic rather than legal mechanism. The economic floor and the reproductive healthcare provision together close that gap.

Gender-Affirming Care

Gender-affirming care is medically necessary healthcare for transgender and nonbinary people. The evidence base is extensive and consistent: access to gender-affirming care produces dramatic improvements in mental health outcomes, reductions in suicidality, and improvements in overall wellbeing. The denial of gender-affirming care produces the opposite outcomes. The restriction of that care by legislation is not a neutral policy choice about the allocation of medical resources. It is the use of law to enforce a singular acceptable body: the body that presents in the gender the state has decided is appropriate based on the characteristics present at birth. It enforces conformity that the medical and psychological communities with expertise in this area do not endorse, against people whose sense of themselves does not match what the dominant culture requires.

Universal healthcare coverage includes gender-affirming care for people of all ages, consistent with the established standards of care developed by the relevant medical and psychological communities. The political interference with medical decision-making in this domain, which has produced legislation in dozens of states restricting care that the relevant medical authorities endorse, is a constitutional violation under the bodily autonomy provision, the equal protection provision, and the due process provision simultaneously.

Disability and Healthcare

The medical model of disability treats disability as a problem located in the individual body that medicine should fix if possible. The social model of disability locates the problem in the mismatch between the built environment, the social structures, and the bodies and minds of the people living in them. The truth contains both: some conditions cause suffering that is intrinsic to the condition and that medicine can alleviate, and some suffering is produced by the failure of the environment to accommodate the full range of human variation.

A healthcare system built on genuine inclusion starts from a different question: not how do we make this person approximate the norm, but what does this person need to live fully, given who they are? The person who uses a wheelchair needs a healthcare system that is physically accessible, that does not require them to be carried up stairs to reach the examination room. The person who is deaf needs a healthcare system that provides interpreting services rather than requiring them to lipread a masked provider. The person with an intellectual disability needs a healthcare system that communicates in ways they can understand and that takes their report of their own symptoms seriously rather than deferring entirely to their caregiver.

Long-term care, the care of people who need ongoing support with the activities of daily living because of age, disability, or chronic condition, is currently funded through a patchwork of Medicare, Medicaid, private insurance, and personal resources that leaves enormous gaps and produces enormous impoverishment. The person who needs long-term care spends down their assets to qualify for Medicaid, which then pays for care at rates that produce inadequate staffing and inadequate quality. Universal healthcare includes long-term care as a covered benefit. The care of people who cannot care for themselves is not a private problem to be solved by families with whatever resources they happen to have. It is a collective responsibility that the collective is obligated to fund.

The Male Default in Medical Science

Medical research has been built predominantly on the study of male bodies. For most of the twentieth century, women were routinely excluded from clinical trials, first informally and then through formal policies justified by concerns about fetal risk and hormonal variability. The practical consequence is that the standard treatments, standard dosages, and standard diagnostic criteria for a wide range of conditions were developed from data collected almost entirely from men and then applied to everyone.

This is not an abstract problem. It has documented consequences for how women are diagnosed and treated. Heart attack symptoms present differently in women than in men, but the symptoms taught in medical training and depicted in public health campaigns are the male presentation. Women having heart attacks are more likely to be sent home from emergency rooms without diagnosis. The diagnostic criteria for conditions from autoimmune diseases to sleep disorders were developed from male populations and perform worse when applied to women. Drug dosages calculated from male body weight and metabolism produce different effects in female bodies, a fact that was not systematically studied until 1993, when the NIH Revitalization Act required the inclusion of women in federally funded clinical research and the FDA lifted its 1977 rule excluding women of childbearing potential from early drug trials. The decades of research conducted before that requirement produced a body of evidence with a built-in gap.

The exclusion was not accidental. It reflected a set of assumptions about whose body was the default human body and whose was a variation requiring special handling. The male body was the standard. The female body was the complicated version. Those assumptions are present in the research literature, in the diagnostic tools built from that literature, and in the clinical training built from those tools. Correcting them requires more than adding women to future studies. It requires actively identifying where the gap has produced inadequate care and investing in the research needed to close it.

What Investment in Female Healthcare Requires

The conditions that affect only or predominantly women have been systematically underfunded relative to their prevalence and their impact on quality of life. Endometriosis affects roughly one in ten women, causes chronic pain that can be disabling, and takes an average of seven to ten years to diagnose. The diagnostic delay is partly a consequence of inadequate research into the condition and partly a consequence of a medical culture in which women's pain is more likely to be attributed to psychological causes or dismissed as normal. The research investment in endometriosis is a fraction of what comparably prevalent conditions affecting men receive.

The same pattern holds across a range of conditions: polycystic ovary syndrome, fibroids, pelvic floor disorders, perimenopause and menopause, postpartum depression, and chronic pain conditions that disproportionately affect women. These conditions are underresearched, undertreated, and underrepresented in medical education relative to their burden on the people who have them. The woman who spends years seeking a diagnosis for a condition that should have been identified quickly, who is told her symptoms are stress or anxiety or normal variation, who adjusts her life around pain the medical system has decided is not a priority: she is experiencing the consequences of a research agenda that did not include her.

This constitution's healthcare provisions require the correction of this gap through specific obligations: research funding allocated in proportion to disease burden across the full population rather than on the basis of which conditions have historically attracted the most investment; diagnostic criteria reviewed and updated to reflect the presentation of conditions in female bodies; medical education that teaches the full range of symptom presentation rather than only the presentation documented in male-default research; and clinical guidelines that reflect the evidence base for female patients specifically rather than extrapolating from male data.

The requirement that women be included in clinical trials, established by the NIH Revitalization Act of 1993 and strengthened in subsequent years, is a floor. This constitution's obligation goes further: not only must women be included in trials, but the data must be analyzed by sex so that differences in response, dosage, and side effects are documented rather than averaged away. The averaged result that looks adequate for the population as a whole can mask significant harm to a subset of that population. The disaggregated result shows what is actually happening.

Maternal Mortality

The United States has the highest maternal mortality rate of any wealthy country, and it is one of the few wealthy countries where the rate has been rising rather than falling. Black women die in childbirth at three times the rate of white women, a disparity that persists across income and education levels and is not explained by differences in access to care alone. The research on this disparity consistently identifies a contributing factor that the data cannot fully capture but that clinicians and researchers have documented: the systematic undertreatment of Black women's pain and the systematic discounting of Black women's reported symptoms by medical providers.

The 1619 Project and subsequent historical scholarship have documented the origins of this pattern in nineteenth-century medical practices that treated Black people as having higher pain tolerance as a justification for conducting procedures without anesthesia. That belief has no scientific basis. It has persisted in measurable form in the attitudes of medical providers today. The medical student who believes, incorrectly, that Black patients feel less pain is more likely to undertreat Black patients' pain. The provider who discounts a Black woman's report of her own symptoms is more likely to miss the warning signs of a preventable complication.

Reducing maternal mortality requires investment in the full range of factors that produce it: adequate prenatal care, adequate staffing of labor and delivery units, the reversal of hospital closures in rural and low-income communities that have left women without access to obstetric care, and the specific training and accountability measures that address the documented disparities in how different patients are treated. It requires that every maternal death be reviewed by an independent body with the authority to identify contributing factors and recommend changes to prevent the next one. Most states have maternal mortality review committees. Most of them are inadequately funded and their recommendations are not binding.

The Transition

The transition from the current system to universal healthcare is politically difficult and administratively complex, but the elements are known. Countries that have made this transition provide the evidence base. The Canadian single-payer system was built from a provincial experiment in Saskatchewan in the 1960s that was then extended nationally. The German multi-payer regulated system achieves universal coverage through a combination of public and private insurers operating under a common regulatory framework. The British National Health Service employs providers directly. Each model has different advantages and different transition requirements. The specific design is a political question. The commitment to universal coverage is a constitutional one.

The transition requires the protection of the people who currently work in the healthcare administration industry whose jobs are eliminated by the simplification of the system. It requires the negotiation of drug prices that the current system has prohibited through the explicit ban on Medicare negotiating pharmaceutical prices, a ban whose only beneficiary is the pharmaceutical industry. It requires capital investment in the physical infrastructure of care in communities that currently lack it: the rural areas without hospitals, the urban communities without primary care providers, the regions where the market has decided care is not profitable enough to provide.

The floor, once established, is not retracted. The care, once provided, is not withdrawn. The person who is sick is treated. That is what the system is for.

Historical Grief and Reparative Justice

← Healthcare · The Floor and the Framework · Criminal Justice and the Carceral System →

What the Earth Carries and What the Law Must Acknowledge

A Companion Document to the Constitution

The Philosophical Foundation

Some losses do not resolve with time. The theft of indigenous land, the centuries of enslaved labor, the systematic exclusion of women, queer people, disabled people, and immigrants from the promises this nation made about itself: these are not events the present has moved beyond. They are conditions in the present, carried forward in bodies, in communities, in landscapes, and in the accumulated structures of who has access to what.

The framework this constitution is built on holds that grief is cumulative, that carrying is collective, and that the work of reckoning does not end on a deadline set by law. The people most directly descended from these losses cannot be asked to perform a recovery they have not experienced. When the nation asks them to, it is not asking for healing. It is asking for the appearance of healing so that everyone else can stop looking.

This document describes what honest institutional acknowledgment of historical grief requires, what reparative justice means in practice, and what an ongoing process of reckoning looks like when it is designed to be genuine rather than symbolic.

What Was Done: The Specific Losses

Indigenous Peoples and the Theft of Land

The land on which the United States exists was taken. That sentence is not contested by serious historians. The mechanisms varied: treaty, war, forced removal, starvation, the deliberate destruction of the food systems on which specific peoples depended. The treaties that were signed were routinely violated when the land they protected became desirable to settlers and the political will to honor them evaporated. The Indian Removal Act of 1830, the forced marches that followed, the reservation system that concentrated people on the least productive land available, the allotment system that broke up reservation land and transferred it to white ownership: these were not the incidental costs of westward expansion. They were the policy.

The federal boarding school system, which the Interior Department's own investigation traced from 1819 through 1969 across more than four hundred schools, operated with the explicit goal of destroying indigenous languages, cultures, family structures, and identities. The motto of the Carlisle Indian Industrial School, the first federally funded boarding school, was "Kill the Indian, save the man." Children were taken from their families, forbidden to speak their languages, punished for practicing their cultures, and in documented cases subjected to abuse, forced labor, and death. The graves of children who did not survive are still being located on school grounds across the country. Several federally run boarding schools still operate today, though under a changed mission. The people whose parents and grandparents were taken are alive. The trauma is not historical. It is present.

The effects are documented consistently in the research on indigenous communities: elevated rates of poverty, substance use, suicide, and disease that are inseparable from the historical conditions that produced them. The Indian Health Service, the federal agency responsible for healthcare for indigenous people as part of treaty obligations, is chronically underfunded at a fraction of what other federal healthcare programs receive per capita. The treaty obligation exists. The funding to honor it never has been adequate.

Enslaved Labor and Its Aftermath

The United States was built with enslaved labor. The cotton economy that financed the industrial development of the North, the agricultural infrastructure of the South, the wealth that became the capital base of American economic expansion: all of it was produced in significant part by people who were legally property, who could not own the product of their labor, whose family relationships had no legal standing, and whose bodies were subject to violence without legal recourse.

The Thirteenth Amendment abolished slavery in 1865 with an exception: it remained legal as punishment for crime. The Black Codes that followed immediately recriminalized Black freedom, and the convict leasing system restored forced labor under the exception the amendment provided. The reconstruction of white supremacy after Reconstruction, through law, through terror, and through the systematic exclusion of Black Americans from the New Deal programs, the GI Bill, and the Federal Housing Administration loans that built the white middle class, continued the effects of slavery by other means.

The wealth gap between Black and white Americans today is the direct and traceable result of these specific policies. The destruction of the Greenwood district of Tulsa in 1921, in which a prosperous Black community was burned by a white mob with the participation of local law enforcement; the systematic redlining of Black neighborhoods by the FHA; the exclusion of domestic workers and agricultural laborers, predominantly Black and Latino, from the original Social Security Act: these were specific government decisions about whose wealth would be protected and whose would be extracted or destroyed. The gap they produced has not closed.

The Eugenics Program

The United States operated a forced sterilization program that targeted people the state had decided should not reproduce: people with disabilities, people with low incomes, Black and brown people, immigrants, and people whose behavior was classified as deviant. The Supreme Court gave it constitutional cover in its 1927 decision in Buck v. Bell, which upheld the forced sterilization of Carrie Buck. That decision has never been formally overturned. Forced sterilizations continued in California prisons as recently as 2010. The people who were sterilized without consent are part of a harm the nation has never formally renounced.

The Exclusion of Women from Economic and Civic Life

Women were excluded from voting until 1920, and the Nineteenth Amendment's passage did not extend voting rights to Black women in the South, where voter suppression effectively continued until the Voting Rights Act of 1965. Women were legally barred from many professions, from jury service, from holding property independently of their husbands, and from credit in their own names until the Equal Credit Opportunity Act of 1974. The economic consequences of generations of exclusion from the accumulation of wealth and professional standing are present in the wage gap, the wealth gap, and the concentration of unpaid caregiving work that persist today.

LGBTQ+ People and the Violence of Criminalization

Homosexuality was classified as a mental illness by the American Psychiatric Association until 1973. Same-sex conduct was criminalized in many states until the Supreme Court's 2003 decision in Lawrence v. Texas. The AIDS crisis of the 1980s killed tens of thousands of people while the federal government deliberately withheld a response, a documented policy choice made by an administration that considered the affected populations expendable. The people who died, the communities that lost them, and the generation that came of age under the terror of the epidemic without government protection represent a loss the nation has not acknowledged.

What Acknowledgment Requires

The truth and reparative justice process established in Article VII is not a one-time event. It is an ongoing institution, funded permanently, operating continuously, and subject to direct democratic oversight by the communities most directly affected. It draws on the models of truth and reconciliation processes from other countries while being honest about what those processes have and have not achieved.

The South African Truth and Reconciliation Commission created a public record that could not be denied and gave many survivors the experience of being heard by an official body. It did not produce economic reparation and did not fully address the structural inequalities apartheid had built. The Canadian Truth and Reconciliation Commission produced ninety-four calls to action documenting what the residential school system had done. Implementation of those calls to action has been slow and incomplete. The lessons are clear: acknowledgment without repair is incomplete, and repair without structural change reproduces the conditions it claims to address.

The process this constitution establishes has four components that operate simultaneously rather than sequentially.

The First Component: The Public Record

The historical record of what was done, to whom, by whom, and with what consequences is documented in full and made publicly accessible. This means the specific policies, the specific decisions, the specific people who made them, and the specific communities who bore the consequences. It includes documents that agencies have classified or withheld. It includes the testimony of survivors and descendants. It is maintained as a living archive, updated as new evidence emerges and as descendants contribute their knowledge of what was carried in families and communities.

The Second Component: Community-Controlled Acknowledgment

The communities most directly affected by each history have genuine authority over how that history is acknowledged. The federal government does not design a single acknowledgment process and impose it on all affected communities. It funds and supports the processes those communities design for themselves. Indigenous nations, Black communities, the descendants of people forcibly sterilized, LGBTQ+ communities, and other affected groups each have the resources and the authority to determine what honest acknowledgment looks like from their perspective. The process is multilingual, community-rooted, and not bounded by a deadline.

The Third Component: Material Repair

Acknowledgment without material repair is the performance of reckoning rather than reckoning itself. The specific forms of material repair are determined through the democratic process, with the affected communities having genuine decision-making power over what repair looks like for them. The framework includes:

Tribal sovereignty honored in full: existing treaties are honored, land held in trust is returned where communities seek its return, and federal obligations under existing treaties are funded at levels adequate to meet them. The Indian Health Service is funded at parity with other federal healthcare programs. Tribal nations have genuine governmental authority over their territories without requiring federal approval for decisions within their sovereign jurisdiction.

Reparations for the descendants of enslaved people: the specific mechanism is developed through the democratic process, with the communities most directly affected having genuine authority over the design. The precedent exists. The United States paid reparations to Japanese Americans interned during World War II, to the survivors of the Tuskegee syphilis study, and to the survivors of other specific documented government wrongs. The scale of the wrong of slavery and its aftermath is larger than any of these precedents. The scale of the repair is proportional.

Restoration for survivors of forced sterilization and their families, where survivors are living: direct compensation and full access to reproductive healthcare and support.

Investment in the communities most directly damaged by specific historical policies: the reservation communities where the Indian Health Service has been underfunded, the neighborhoods redlined by federal policy, the communities destroyed by the war on drugs, the places where the cumulative burden of specific government decisions is most visible in the present landscape.

The Fourth Component: Structural Change

Reparative justice that does not change the structures that produced the harm will need to be repeated. The structural changes are the other companion documents to this constitution: the criminal justice provisions that address the racial construction of the carceral system, the economic floor that addresses the wealth gap, the healthcare provisions that address Indian Health Service underfunding and documented disparities in how Black patients are treated by the medical system, the voting rights provisions that address the suppression of Black and indigenous votes, the education provisions that address curriculum erasure and the school-to-prison pipeline. The truth and reparative justice process is not separate from these structural changes. It is the honest account of why they are necessary.

On the Objection That It Is Too Long Ago

The most common objection to reparative justice is that the wrongs occurred too long ago: the people who committed them are dead, the people most directly harmed are dead, and the current generation cannot be held responsible for what their ancestors did. This objection misunderstands what reparative justice is addressing.

The wealth gap between Black and white Americans is not the product of events that ended in 1865. It is the product of specific government decisions made in the twentieth century. Many of the people directly affected by redlining, by exclusion from the GI Bill, by the destruction of specific communities, are alive. Many more are the direct children and grandchildren of people who were affected.

The underfunding of the Indian Health Service is not a historical wrong. It is a current wrong, renewed in each budget cycle. The treaties that were violated are not old documents with no current legal standing. They are binding legal agreements that the United States has continued to violate.

The question is not whether the loss is present. It is. The question is whether the institution is honest about what it knows.

On the Objection That It Divides Rather Than Unites

The second common objection is that focusing on historical wrongs divides the nation rather than uniting it. This objection has the causation backwards. The division is produced by the unaddressed wrong, not by addressing it. The nation that asks the people most directly affected by historical violence to absorb that violence quietly in the interest of national unity is not asking for unity. It is asking for silence.

Honest acknowledgment of what happened, material repair of what can be repaired, and structural change that prevents the reproduction of the same patterns: this is what unity on honest terms requires. Unity that requires some people to pretend they have not been harmed is not unity.

The Ongoing Process

The truth and reparative justice process does not have an end date. What it has is a structure: permanent funding, community authority, democratic oversight, and the commitment to honesty about what is known and what remains to be known.

Security and the Common Defense

← Media and Information · The Floor and the Framework · From the Floor to the Charter →

What Security Actually Means and How to Build It

A Companion Document to the Constitution

The Philosophical Foundation

Security means the protection of people's actual ability to live full lives. It means food, housing, healthcare, education, bodily autonomy, environmental safety, and freedom from violence. It does not mean the projection of military or economic dominance over other countries. A nation that can destroy any enemy but cannot house its own people is not a secure nation. It has confused the instruments of security with security itself.

The United States currently spends more on its military than the next ten countries combined. It has been in continuous armed conflict somewhere in the world for most of its existence. Its veterans return home to inadequate healthcare, high rates of suicide, and difficulty accessing the economic floor the country sent them to defend. The communities that send the most people into the military are often the communities with the fewest economic alternatives. The construction of military spending as national security, presented as obvious and necessary, is a political choice. This document examines what that choice has cost and what a different choice would look like.

The Use of Military Force

The decision to use military force in the name of the nation belongs to the nation's representatives, accountable to the nation's people. The Constitution of 1787 gave Congress the power to declare war for exactly this reason: the people who bear the cost of war should have a voice in the decision to wage it. That principle has been eroded steadily since World War II. The United States has fought major sustained conflicts in Korea, Vietnam, Iraq, and Afghanistan without a formal declaration of war. The Authorization for Use of Military Force passed after September 11, 2001 has been used to justify military operations in countries never contemplated when it was written, without further Congressional approval.

This constitution restores the original principle with specific mechanisms. The use of military force requires a declaration of war by Congress. Emergency deployments are permitted for up to thirty days without Congressional approval, after which Congress must vote to authorize the continuation of the deployment or it ends. The people may trigger a referendum on any sustained military commitment through the initiative process established in Article I. The President who commits forces to sustained combat without Congressional authorization is in violation of this constitution and subject to removal.

This is not a pacifist provision. It is a democratic one. The nation may defend itself. The nation may honor treaty obligations to allies. The nation may respond to genuine emergencies. All of these things can happen within a framework that requires democratic accountability for the decision to use violence in the nation's name.

The Military-Industrial Complex

Companies that profit from military contracts have a financial interest in the expansion of military spending regardless of whether that expansion serves the national interest. The relationship between those companies and the elected and appointed officials who make decisions about military spending is one of the most thoroughly documented sources of corruption in American public life. Defense contractors fund congressional campaigns. Retired military officers move into defense industry employment. The officials who approve contracts have financial relationships with the companies whose contracts they approve.

This constitution's transparency provisions apply to military contracting with full force. Every lobbying contact between defense contractors and elected or appointed officials is a matter of public record within forty-eight hours. Campaign contributions from defense contractors are subject to the same caps and disclosure requirements as all other contributions. The movement of military leaders directly into employment with defense companies they previously worked with is prohibited for a defined period after leaving government service. Contracts are awarded through a transparent competitive process subject to independent audit.

The argument that these relationships are necessary because defense contracting is too complex for ordinary transparency requirements is the same argument every concentrated interest makes for its own exemption. It is not a sufficient argument. The public interest in knowing how military spending decisions are made outweighs the industry's interest in making them quietly.

Peace-Building as a Constitutional Obligation

Article IX establishes peace-building, conflict prevention, and the systems that support negotiation and peaceful resolution of conflict as constitutional obligations, funded at a defined ratio relative to military spending. This document defines what that means in practice.

The research on conflict prevention is consistent: the conditions that produce armed conflict are knowable and addressable before violence begins. Poverty, resource scarcity, political exclusion, historical grievances without legitimate outlets, and the presence of armed groups with more resources than the governments they operate alongside: these are the documented precursors of armed conflict. The investment in addressing these conditions before they produce violence is less expensive by every measure than the investment in military response after violence has begun.

The United States currently spends a small fraction of its national security budget on the diplomatic and development tools that address conflict precursors. The State Department and the United States Agency for International Development together receive less than one-tenth of what the Department of Defense receives. This allocation reflects a construction of what security requires that this constitution rejects: the assumption that military capacity is the primary instrument of security and everything else is supplementary.

The rebalanced allocation this constitution requires does not eliminate military capacity. It funds the full range of instruments that genuine security requires: diplomacy, development assistance, conflict mediation, support for democratic institutions in fragile states, and the international legal frameworks that provide alternatives to violence for the resolution of disputes between nations.

The United States' relationship to international law and international institutions has been inconsistent at best. It has selectively participated in international frameworks when they served its interests and withdrawn from them when they did not. This constitution establishes consistent engagement with international legal frameworks as a constitutional obligation, not a policy preference subject to reversal by each administration. The nation that helped build the post-World War II international order and then periodically undermined it when the order constrained its own behavior has not been a reliable partner in the project of replacing war with law. That changes here.

The Just War Principle

Not all use of force is prohibited by this constitution. The just war tradition, developed over centuries of moral and legal philosophy, provides a framework for distinguishing the use of force that can be justified from the use of force that cannot. The core principles are: the cause must be just; the decision must be made by legitimate authority accountable to the people; force must be a last resort after other means have been exhausted; the harm caused must be proportionate to the good achieved; and the means used must distinguish between combatants and civilians.

These principles are not new. They are incorporated into the international humanitarian law that the United States has ratified. What this constitution adds is the enforcement mechanism: military actions that violate these principles are subject to constitutional challenge, the officials who ordered them are subject to accountability under the due process provisions of Article VII, and the people may use the referendum mechanism to review any sustained military commitment.

The drone strike program, which has killed documented numbers of civilians in countries with which the United States is not formally at war, fails the proportionality and civilian distinction tests of the just war framework. The detention of people without charge or trial at Guantanamo Bay fails the due process provisions of Article VII. These are not novel legal conclusions. They are the application of principles this constitution makes enforceable that were previously aspirational.

The Conversion Framework

Article IX establishes that existing military capacity is progressively redirected toward the obligations this constitution has already established. This document defines what that conversion looks like in practice.

The United States military has capabilities that the country desperately needs applied to non-military problems. The Army Corps of Engineers has the capacity to build infrastructure at scale. The military's logistics systems can move people and supplies to disaster areas faster than any civilian agency. Military research and development has produced technologies, including the internet, GPS, and many medical advances, that transformed civilian life. The military's medical infrastructure is among the most sophisticated in the world.

Conversion means directing these existing capabilities toward the constitutional obligations this document has established. Specifically:

The Army Corps of Engineers and military construction capacity are redirected toward climate resilience infrastructure: the sea walls, the flood management systems, the water infrastructure, the grid modernization that the environmental rights provision requires. The communities most at risk from climate change, which are disproportionately the communities with the least resources to protect themselves, receive priority.

The military's logistics and transportation capacity is integrated into the federal disaster response system, with clear protocols for deployment that do not require the declaration of martial law or the suspension of civilian authority. The inadequacy of the federal response to Hurricane Katrina in 2005, when the military's capacity sat largely unused while people died, is the failure this integration is designed to prevent.

Military medical infrastructure is integrated into the universal healthcare system, beginning with the Veterans Administration, which is brought to full funding and full staffing and opened to the communities surrounding military installations where the VA is often the only substantial medical facility.

Military research and development is reoriented toward the clean energy transition. The military already has strong institutional reasons to pursue energy independence: fuel supply lines are a significant source of military vulnerability, and installations that can generate their own power are more resilient. The research investment that pursues these goals for military reasons produces civilian applications that accelerate the broader clean energy transition.

Conversion is not the elimination of military capacity. It is the recognition that the country has invested enormous resources in capabilities that can serve the full range of constitutional obligations rather than only the military ones. The question is whether those capabilities are deployed in the public interest. This constitution says they are.

Veterans

The people who serve in the military bear the direct personal cost of the security decisions this document is redesigning. The treatment of veterans by the country that sent them to war is the clearest measure of whether the country's stated values about service and sacrifice are genuine or ceremonial.

The Veterans Administration healthcare system is chronically underfunded and understaffed relative to the need it is supposed to serve. Veterans wait months for appointments. Mental health services are inadequate to the documented need. The suicide rate among veterans is significantly higher than among the general population. The country that sends people to war and then provides inadequate care for the psychological and physical damage war produces is not honoring its obligations. It is managing them at the minimum level consistent with political viability.

This constitution's universal healthcare provision covers veterans with the same comprehensive coverage it provides to everyone, with the VA system expanded and fully funded as the delivery mechanism for veterans who prefer to use it. The economic floor provisions apply to veterans with full force: the veteran who returns from service to unemployment, housing instability, and inadequate healthcare is not a personal failure story. They are the evidence of what happens when the country treats the cost of service as a private problem rather than a collective obligation.

Nuclear Weapons

The United States maintains a nuclear arsenal capable of destroying human civilization multiple times over. The cost of maintaining that arsenal, the research, the delivery systems, the command and control infrastructure, the ongoing modernization program, runs to hundreds of billions of dollars over the current planning period. The doctrine governing the use of these weapons has varied across administrations and is not subject to democratic oversight in any meaningful way. The President of the United States can order the launch of nuclear weapons without the approval of Congress, without judicial review, and without the possibility of recall once the order is given.

This constitution does not unilaterally disarm the United States. It establishes that nuclear weapons policy is subject to the same democratic accountability as all other security policy: Congressional authorization for any change in nuclear posture, full transparency about the doctrine governing use, and active participation in international frameworks for nuclear reduction and eventual elimination. The goal of a world without nuclear weapons is a constitutional commitment, not an aspiration. The path toward it is through negotiated multilateral reduction, pursued with the same seriousness the country applies to military expansion.

The Transition

The transition from the current security framework to the one this document describes is politically difficult because the current framework has powerful institutional defenders. The defense industry, the military services, the members of Congress whose districts host military installations and defense contractors: all have interests in the continuation of the current allocation of resources. Those interests are not illegitimate. The people who work in defense industries and military communities have real stakes in how the transition is managed.

The transition requires a timeline that allows communities dependent on military spending to develop alternative economic bases, with the federal investment in conversion providing the economic activity that replaces what the drawdown removes. The communities that have hosted military installations and defense industries have often done so at significant cost to their environments and their civic life. They are owed a transition that takes that cost seriously.

Citizenship and Immigration

← Voting and Electoral Systems · The Floor and the Framework · Healthcare →

Belonging, Presence, and the Obligation of History

A Companion Document to the Constitution

The Philosophical Foundation

Citizenship as it currently operates is a system that presents itself as natural law. The line between citizen and non-citizen, between the person whose presence is legitimate and the person whose presence is illegal, was drawn by the people who were already inside it, encoding their interests as the condition of belonging. That line has moved many times in American history, always in the direction of excluding the people whose inclusion was most politically inconvenient for the people doing the excluding. The Chinese Exclusion Act. The national origins quota system, which from 1924 to 1965 set strict caps on immigration from Southern and Eastern Europe, Asia, and Africa while favoring Northern and Western Europeans. The systematic exclusion of people from countries whose governments the United States found threatening. The construction of the undocumented person as criminal rather than as a person whose circumstances the law has failed to accommodate.

This is a system that presents its own choices as the natural order of things. The citizen is real. The non-citizen is the deviation from the real. That framing is a political choice made by people with the power to make it. It can be remade. The question is not whether to have a system of membership and belonging. Communities require that. The question is what the system is built on: the bureaucratic achievement of a legal category, or presence and subjection to law as the foundation of belonging.

The answer this document builds from is the second. The person who lives here, works here, raises children here, pays taxes here, is arrested under laws made here, buries the dead here, builds the relationships and community that constitute a life here: that person belongs here. The paperwork has not kept up with the belonging. The obligation runs to the person, not the paperwork.

Citizenship: Three Paths

Birthright

Every person born on this soil is a citizen. This is the current rule and it is the right rule. The Fourteenth Amendment, passed after the Civil War to ensure that the descendants of enslaved people could not be denied citizenship, established it precisely because the alternative, citizenship contingent on the citizenship of one’s parents, was the mechanism that had been used to exclude them. The effort to end birthright citizenship is not a neutral policy proposal. It is the attempt to restore the mechanism the Fourteenth Amendment was written to destroy. It is a demand to return to a system the country already tried and already repudiated.

Naturalization

Naturalization is currently a process designed as an obstacle course. The fees, which can exceed a thousand dollars and are not waived for people who cannot pay them. The wait times, which run to years and in some categories to decades. The English language requirement, which has no functional relationship to the capacity for democratic participation and significant relationship to the national origin of the applicant. The civics test, which asks questions about American history and government that the majority of native-born citizens could not answer. The discretion given to individual officers that produces wildly inconsistent outcomes for similarly situated applicants.

The naturalization process should be accessible, affordable, timely, and designed to receive the person rather than to exclude them. The language requirement is replaced by language support: the government provides translation and interpretation throughout the process. The civics requirement is replaced by a civic orientation: not a test but a conversation, an introduction to the rights and responsibilities of membership conducted in a spirit of welcome rather than gatekeeping. The fees are eliminated or income-adjusted. The wait times are addressed by adequate staffing and resources. The discretion that produces inconsistency is constrained by clear standards and robust appeal rights.

Long-Term Residency

The person who has lived here for a defined continuous period, who has built a life here, who is subject to the laws here, belongs here in every meaningful sense. The bureaucratic category of undocumented does not change the fact of belonging. It only names the gap between the belonging and the legal recognition of it. The obligation runs to closing that gap, not to enforcing it.

The specific period is a political question to be determined through the democratic process. The principle is not: it is the recognition that presence and community membership over time constitute a form of belonging that the legal system is obligated to recognize. The ten million or more people currently living in this country without legal status are not a problem to be solved through enforcement. They are people whose belonging has not been legally recognized, a failure of the legal system that the legal system is obligated to correct.

Indigenous Sovereignty

Indigenous peoples’ relationship to this land precedes the nation that now administers it by thousands of years. The framework of immigration and citizenship that applies to everyone else does not apply to people whose nations predate the nation that is now asking them to prove they belong. They are not immigrants on their own land. Their sovereignty is not a concession made by the federal government that the federal government can revoke. It is a political fact that predates the federal government and that the federal government is obligated to honor.

The history of federal Indian law is a history of the systematic violation of treaty obligations, the unilateral breaking of agreements made in the name of the nation, the forced assimilation of indigenous people into the dominant culture through educational and religious institutions, and the appropriation of indigenous land through legal mechanisms designed to produce that outcome while maintaining the appearance of legitimacy. The historical reckoning provision of the constitution names this history. The tribal sovereignty provision names the obligation it generates. This document adds the specific content of that obligation: every treaty made with every tribal nation is honored in full. Where treaties have been violated, the obligation to remedy the violation is active and ongoing. Tribal nations have the same standing in federal courts as states. The federal government’s obligation to tribal nations, a legal duty of care established by treaty and law, is treated as a genuine and enforceable commitment, not a rhetorical gesture.

It is worth noting that federal recognition of tribal nations is itself a bureaucratic category with a contested history: many indigenous communities exist and have always existed without having received or sought federal recognition, and the absence of that designation does not diminish the reality of their presence, history, or sovereignty.

The recognition of tribal citizenship alongside American citizenship, for members of tribal nations, is not a complication of the citizenship framework. It is the honest acknowledgment that this nation exists within a prior political landscape that it did not create and cannot erase. Two legitimate political identities coexisting without requiring one to eliminate the other.

The Asylum System

The Obligation of History

People do not abandon their homes and communities without cause. The causes are knowable: violence, persecution, poverty so extreme that survival requires leaving, environmental catastrophe, the collapse of the conditions that make ordinary life possible. Many of those causes are traceable to the decisions of this government. The coups supported, the governments destabilized, the trade agreements that destroyed local economies, the climate emissions that are making parts of the world uninhabitable. The nation that helped produce the conditions from which people are fleeing has an obligation toward those people that exceeds the current asylum framework.

The current framework asks: does this person face persecution on account of race, religion, nationality, membership in a particular social group, or political opinion? The question was written in the 1951 Refugee Convention, an international agreement drafted in the aftermath of World War II for a specific historical context, and has not kept pace with the actual causes of displacement in the current world. Climate displacement is not covered. Economic devastation produced by external trade policy is not covered. The violence of gangs and cartels that operate in the instability created by decades of failed drug policy is variably covered depending on which judge reviews the claim. The framework has become a filtering mechanism that excludes the people whose need is most urgent and most directly connected to the decisions of this government.

The rebuilt system starts from the question: what caused this person to leave, and what is this nation’s relationship to that cause? The answer determines the obligation. The person fleeing a government this nation supported has a stronger claim than the current framework recognizes. The person fleeing climate conditions this nation’s emissions contributed to has a claim the current framework does not recognize at all. The obligation is proportional to the causation and the causation is documented.

Humane Processing

No person seeking asylum or entry is held in conditions that violate the freedom from cruel punishment provision of the constitution. The detention centers that currently operate with conditions documented as cruel, degrading, and dangerous are closed. Processing is conducted in the community, with the person released to sponsors or community organizations while their claim is reviewed. The review is timely: not the years-long backlog that currently functions in practice as a denial for many applicants, but a process adequately staffed to reach decisions within months.

The person seeking entry is a full person with a full history. The processing system is built to receive that history rather than to sort the person into a category as rapidly as possible. Legal representation is provided: the asylum seeker without a lawyer is denied at rates that document the effect of legal representation on outcomes in a system too complex to navigate alone. The provision of counsel is not charity. It is the constitutional guarantee of fair process applied to the people most directly subject to its protections. Due process, in plain terms, means that a person subject to a legal decision has the right to understand the process, to be heard, and to have their case decided fairly. The asylum seeker is entitled to that. The current system frequently denies it.

Children

No child is separated from their family as a mechanism of deterrence or enforcement. The separation of children from parents as a policy tool is the cruelest available expression of the state’s power over the people who have the least: I will take what you love most if you cross this line. It is a constitutional violation under the bodily autonomy provision, the freedom from cruel punishment provision, and the due process provision simultaneously. It has no legitimate policy justification. It is deterrence through the deliberate infliction of trauma on children, and it is named here as what it is.

Children who were brought to this country before the age of legal decision-making, who were raised here, educated here, who have no meaningful connection to any other country, are citizens. The argument that they should be deported to countries they do not remember, whose languages they may not speak, to suffer for decisions made by their parents before they were old enough to make decisions, is the enforcement of a legal fiction at the expense of a human reality. The law has not caught up with the life. The obligation runs to the life.

Voting Rights and Residency

The vote is the mechanism by which the people governed by a law have a voice in the law. The person who lives here, works here, pays taxes here, sends children to school here, and is subject to arrest under laws made here is governed by those laws. The withholding of the vote from that person on the grounds that they have not achieved a particular bureaucratic status is the original grievance of this nation’s founding, applied to the people whose labor has been most essential to the nation’s functioning and whose political voice has been most consistently suppressed.

Voting rights for all residents subject to the laws, not citizens alone, is the honest application of the principle that the people are the government. Several American cities already practice this at the local level. The extension to state and federal elections requires the constitutional provision already established and the political will to implement it against the resistance of people whose power depends on the exclusion of the people who would vote against it. That resistance is not a neutral democratic objection. It is the defense of a system that serves specific interests, presented as the natural order of things.

The Transition

The transition from the current immigration system to this one is political before it is administrative. The current system has enormous institutional inertia, an enforcement apparatus of significant size, and a set of financial interests that profit from its continuation: the private prison industry that operates immigration detention facilities, the contractors who build the infrastructure of enforcement, the political actors whose constituencies are organized around the construction of the immigrant as threat.

The transition requires the simultaneous dismantling of the enforcement architecture that is inconsistent with this document’s principles and the construction of the processing and support infrastructure that the new system requires. It requires giving legal status to people currently living without legal recognition. It requires rebuilding the relationship with the countries from which most unauthorized migration originates: not through enforcement agreements but through foreign aid and investment, fair trade policy, and the climate action that would address the conditions producing displacement.

None of this is simple. All of it is necessary. The person who has been here for twenty years, who has raised children here, who has built a business here, who has been a member of a community here in every sense except the legal one: that person is waiting for the legal system to catch up with the reality the legal system has failed to recognize. The obligation to close that gap is not charitable. It is constitutional.
