Education

← Women, Children, and the Unpaid Economy · The Floor and the Framework · The Abolition of Private Schooling →

What It Is For and How to Build It

A Companion Document to the Constitution

The Philosophical Foundation

Education is not primarily workforce preparation. It is not even primarily civic preparation in the thin sense of knowing the three branches of government and showing up to vote. It is the cultivation of people who can stay in a room with complexity without demanding its premature resolution, who can hold more than one identity at the same time without requiring one to silence all the others, who can recognize that their understanding of the world is shaped by their particular experience without being destroyed by that recognition.

That is a different educational philosophy than anything currently operating at scale in American public education. The current system is organized around the singular acceptable student: the student who scores within the acceptable range on the acceptable measures, who progresses through the acceptable sequence at the acceptable pace, who produces the acceptable outputs in the acceptable formats. The student who exceeds or escapes these categories in any direction is managed back toward the center. The student who cannot be managed back is sorted into a remedial category and the sorting is presented as an objective finding about the student rather than a judgment made by a system built without them in mind.

Obsessions are the fuel for inquiry, research, and investigation. That is an educational philosophy. It names the thing the current system is most systematically designed to extinguish: the obsession, the particular burning interest that does not fit the sequence, that exceeds the time allotted, that insists on going deeper when the curriculum needs to move on. The student with an obsession is a management problem. A different philosophy says the obsession is the condition without which genuine learning cannot happen. The current system has it exactly backwards.

The Structural Critique

Funding and the Zip Code

American public schools are funded primarily through local property taxes. This means that the quality of the public school a child attends is determined by the wealth of the neighborhood in which they were born. This is not an accidental outcome of a neutral system. It is the intended outcome of a system designed to ensure that the children of the affluent receive better-resourced schooling than the children of everyone else, while maintaining the fiction that all children have equal access to public education.

This pattern shows itself directly here: a structure of equal opportunity, presented as the natural order, that encodes the interests of the people who built it. The zip code is not a neutral administrative category. It is a sorting mechanism. The child born in the wealthy suburb and the child born in the post-industrial city are not receiving the same public education. They are receiving educations whose resource gap reflects and reproduces the wealth gap that produced it. The system is self-perpetuating. It requires no conspiracy to maintain. It only requires the continued acceptance of property tax funding as simply how school finance works.

Federal equalization funding exists but is inadequate and subject to the political will of each Congress. A constitutional obligation to equalize resources across all public schools removes the question from political negotiation. The floor of educational resource is the same for every child regardless of where they were born. This is not redistribution in the pejorative sense. It is the honest application of the equal protection principle to the domain where inequality is most consequential and most durable.

Standardized Testing as the Singular Acceptable Student

The standardized test is where the problem shows itself most clearly in education policy. It is a construction of what intelligence and preparation look like, built from studies of a specific population and administered as though it measures something universal and objective. It does not. It measures performance on a particular kind of task, under particular conditions, by people whose prior education has prepared them for that particular kind of task under those particular conditions. The correlation between test scores and family income is not a surprising finding. It is the predictable outcome of a test that measures, in significant part, the quality of the preparation that wealth makes possible.

The consequences of the test determine access to resources: to advanced coursework, to college admission, to the credential that opens the door to the next credential. The child sorted into the remedial category by the test does not receive more support. They receive less. The sorting mechanism produces the outcome it predicts by withholding from the students who most need investment the investment that would most change their trajectory. The accumulated disadvantage is built into the structure, reproduced generation by generation, presented as the natural result of who the students are rather than as a political choice about whose children deserve resources.

Assessment that serves education rather than sorting asks different questions. Not: how does this student perform relative to the population the test was built around? But: what does this student know, what can they do, what are they building toward, and what do they need next? Portfolio assessment, project-based evaluation, demonstrated competency, teacher observation over time: these are not soft alternatives to rigorous measurement. They are more rigorous, because they measure the actual complexity of what a student knows rather than the subset of that knowledge that can be captured in a timed multiple-choice format.

The School-to-Prison Pipeline

The school-to-prison pipeline is the criminal legal system, starting in childhood. The mechanisms are well documented: zero-tolerance discipline policies that treat childhood behavior as criminal conduct, police presence in schools that routes disciplinary matters into the criminal legal system, suspension and expulsion that remove students from education and deposit them in the conditions that produce further involvement with the criminal system, special education placements that segregate and stigmatize rather than support. These mechanisms fall disproportionately on Black and brown students, on students with disabilities, on students whose behavior reflects trauma rather than defiance.

The pipeline is the nation's accumulated history of harm made visible in schools: the losses built into the foundation of this country, reproduced in the institution nominally designed to offer the next generation a different outcome. The school that responds to the traumatized child with punishment rather than support is the school that has decided in advance that this child's presence in the educational community is conditional. The condition is compliance. The threat issued to eight-year-olds: be the acceptable student or be removed. The removal is not the end of the story. It is the beginning of the next chapter in a story the system has already decided how to tell.

Restorative practices in schools, investment in counselors and social workers rather than police officers, and a trauma-informed approach to behavior that asks what happened to this child rather than what is wrong with this child: these are not soft on discipline. They are the practice of staying in the room with the difficult child rather than removing them. Bringing the full weight of attention to what is actually there rather than managing it out of sight.

The Curriculum as Curated Consensus Reality

The curriculum is not a neutral collection of the most important things to know. It is a selection made by people with the power to select, encoding their construction of what counts as knowledge, whose history matters, whose literary tradition is universal, whose scientific contributions are canonical. Feminist scholarship of the past fifty years has documented this pattern in detail: the curriculum built from studies of men and boys and presented as universal, the literary canon defined by the critics who defined it and called the definition objective, the history that centers the experiences of the people who wrote it.

This is not a problem that is solved by adding a diversity unit. Treating excluded knowledge as an add-on is its own version of the same problem: the dominant curriculum remains the curriculum, and the additions are positioned as supplements to the real thing rather than as challenges to the construction of what the real thing is. The full integration of the complete human record requires not adding to the current curriculum but rebuilding it from the ground up with the question: what do we know about how human beings have lived, created, organized themselves, resisted, built, and lost, across the full range of human experience? The answer to that question is a different curriculum than the one currently taught.

Indigenous knowledge systems, feminist scholarship on how knowledge is built and who gets to build it, the intellectual traditions of the African diaspora, the history of labor and the people who performed it, the history of what was done to the people the dominant history needed to not see: these are not supplements. They are the complete record that the current curriculum is incomplete without. The student who graduates from a public school having learned only the consensus version of human history has not received an education. They have received an incomplete picture designed to look like the whole thing.

Early Childhood

The research on early childhood education is among the most robust in all of social science. The Perry Preschool Project, which followed participants for over fifty years across their whole lives, found that high-quality early childhood education produces measurable benefits across the full life course: higher graduation rates, higher employment, lower involvement with the criminal legal system, better health outcomes, greater civic participation. The Abecedarian Project, which began working with children in infancy rather than at age three, shows similar findings with even earlier intervention. The Chicago Child-Parent Centers, which ran across a larger and more diverse urban population over many years, extended the evidence with consistent results.

The benefits are largest for children from low-income families. This is not because early childhood education matters less for affluent children. It is because affluent children are already receiving the equivalent through the resources their families can provide: the books, the conversation, the stable housing, the nutritious food, the absence of chronic stress. The public investment in early childhood education for children whose families cannot provide these conditions is the economic floor applied at the moment when the floor matters most, before the gap between children born into different circumstances has had years to compound.

Universal pre-K from age three, fully funded and fully resourced, is not an educational luxury. It is the precondition for everything the educational system claims to be trying to achieve. The child who arrives at kindergarten two years behind a peer who had access to high-quality early childhood education is not going to catch up through the normal operation of the K-12 system. The gap compounds. The investment that does not happen at three requires ten times the investment at thirteen to begin to close. You build at the beginning because the beginning is where the building matters most.

The Teacher

Any serious document about education has to address who teaches and under what conditions. The current system treats teachers the way it treats students: as people to be managed into compliance rather than trusted as professionals in their own classrooms. Scripted curricula that require teachers to follow a script regardless of what the students in front of them need. Test-prep mandates that compress the curriculum into the subset of knowledge that will be assessed. Evaluation systems that reduce the complex practice of teaching to a score derived from student test performance. Administrative hierarchies that increase while classroom resources decrease.

The teacher who is not permitted to follow their own obsessions cannot teach students to follow theirs. The teaching philosophy this document holds to is simple: bring everything you know into the room and give it completely. The full weight of attention. No holding back for a more manageable version. The teacher who is managing thirty students through a scripted curriculum toward a standardized test is not doing that. They are a production line worker whose product is test scores.

Teacher pay, in every country where it has been studied, is correlated with educational outcomes. Countries that pay teachers comparably to other professions requiring similar education and expertise attract a broader and stronger pool of candidates into the profession. The United States systematically underpays teachers, particularly at the elementary level and in the schools serving the lowest-income communities: the schools where the teaching is hardest and the support is least. This is the same pattern applied to labor policy: a judgment about whose work is valuable, presented as the market's objective assessment of what teaching is worth.

Teacher autonomy is the prerequisite for the teaching this document envisions. The teacher trusted to know their students, to follow the thread when the students pull it somewhere the curriculum did not anticipate, to spend three weeks on the thing that has caught the class's obsession rather than moving on because the sequence requires it: that teacher is doing the real work. That teacher cannot exist inside the current accountability architecture. The architecture has to change.

Universal Design and Neurodiversity

Universal design in education starts from the question: how do we build this so that every student can participate fully, rather than building it for the median student and then providing accommodations for everyone else? The accommodation model treats the standard as fixed and offers a lesser version to everyone who cannot meet it. The universal design model asks: what if we built the standard differently from the beginning, so that the modification is not necessary?

The neurodiversity framework understands cognitive difference not as deficit but as variation. The student with dyslexia is not a student with a broken reading mechanism. They are a student whose reading mechanism works differently from the one the current instructional system was designed for. The student with ADHD is not a student with deficient attention. They are a student whose attention works differently from the one the current classroom structure was designed for. The mismatch between the student and the system is a design problem, not a student problem.

Multiple means of representation: students access information through different modalities and the curriculum is built to offer multiple pathways into the same content. Multiple means of expression: students demonstrate what they know through different formats and assessment systems are built to receive multiple forms of demonstration. Multiple means of engagement: students are motivated by different things and the learning environment is built to activate different forms of interest and persistence. These are the Universal Design for Learning principles developed by researchers at CAST (the Center for Applied Special Technology), and they are the honest acknowledgment that there is no singular acceptable learner and the system built for one is failing everyone else.

Education and Historical Grief

The history of American education is inseparable from the history of American violence against specific populations. The boarding school system for indigenous children, which operated for over a century with the explicit goal of destroying indigenous languages, cultures, and family structures, is not a distant historical episode. Its effects are present in indigenous communities today in the patterns of trauma, disconnection, and loss that researchers and community members document consistently. Several federally run boarding schools still operate today, though under a changed mission. The people whose grandparents were taken are alive.

The systematic miseducation of Black children, documented from Carter G. Woodson's 1933 book "The Mis-Education of the Negro" forward, is education used as a tool of erasure: the teaching of a version of history and culture that positioned Black people as objects of history rather than its subjects, that excluded or distorted the intellectual and creative traditions of the African diaspora, that prepared Black students for the subordinate positions the economy had decided they would occupy. The curriculum integration that followed the civil rights movement was incomplete and has been progressively rolled back in many states.

The truth and restorative justice process established in Article VII of the Constitution must include an educational component: the honest reckoning with what the educational system did and did not do to specific communities, and the active reconstruction of an educational system that those communities have genuine power to shape. This is not the dominant system adding a unit on indigenous history written by people outside indigenous communities. It is indigenous communities, Black communities, the communities most directly affected by the educational system's historical violence, having genuine authority over the education of their children. That authority is not a supplement to the constitutional education right. It is its fullest expression.

What the Classroom Looks Like

The classroom is recognizable as a classroom. There are students and a teacher. There is content to be learned. There is assessment of whether the learning is happening. None of that changes. What changes is the relationship between all of those elements.

The content is the full human record, not the curated consensus version. The students bring their own histories into contact with it, which means the content is alive in the room rather than delivered from outside it. The teacher is following the obsessions rather than the sequence, which means the sequence emerges from the learning rather than being imposed on it. The assessment asks what the student knows and can do and is building toward, not how they compare to the students the test was designed to measure.

The room holds everyone. The student who reads differently, who attends differently, who processes differently, who grieves differently, who carries a history that the curriculum has previously pretended does not exist: all of them are in the room and the room is built to hold all of them. Not because inclusion is a value to be performed but because the capacity to engage with complexity cannot be cultivated in a room from which complexity has been sorted away.

The student in this classroom is learning to stay in the room with difficulty. Not to be comfortable with everything, not to agree with everyone, not to perform tolerance as a social courtesy. To genuinely engage with what is actually there, including what is uncomfortable, including what challenges their own understanding of how things are. That is the civic capacity the constitution requires. It cannot be taught in a lecture. It can only be practiced in a room where it is required.

The teacher in this classroom brings the full weight of attention to what is actually happening in the room, following the thread when it leads somewhere unexpected, trusting the process. Not managing the students toward a predetermined output but accompanying them toward something neither the teacher nor the students have fully seen yet.

The classroom built on this philosophy gives students the same gift: the time and permission to find out how much is actually in the room they are in.

The Transition

The transition from the current system to this one is not instantaneous and pretending it could be would be dishonest. The current system employs millions of people, maintains physical infrastructure across the country, carries institutional inertia of enormous weight, and is defended by interests that benefit from its current form: the testing industry, the textbook industry, the private school sector, the real estate interests that depend on the connection between school quality and property values.

The transition requires a timeline, adequate funding, and the genuine participation of the communities most affected in designing what replaces what currently exists. It requires the training and compensation of teachers for the practices this document describes. It requires the physical reconstruction of school buildings designed for the singular acceptable student into spaces that can hold everyone. It requires the development of curriculum that does not yet exist at the scale required. None of this is impossible. All of it is expensive. The expense is the investment that makes everything else possible.

The abolition of private schools requires the same honest acknowledgment of transition complexity. The endowments, the buildings, the teachers, the families who have organized their lives around private school options: all of these require a transition plan that is fair to the people caught in the change while being uncompromising about the destination. The destination is a public school system good enough that no family needs a private option and wealthy enough to make that genuine rather than aspirational.

What is written here is one pass: it finds what the previous conversations walked past, it builds on what the constitution gestured at, and it points toward a next pass that will find what this one has missed.

From the Floor to the Charter

← Security and the Common Defense · The Floor and the Framework

Adapting the Constitution for State and Local Governance

A companion document to The Floor and the Framework

Introduction: The National Floor and the Local Work

The constitution described in The Floor and the Framework is a national document. It establishes the minimum: the floor below which no level of government may push any person, with no ceiling on the rights a state or city may add. But the floor is not the whole building. States have constitutions. Counties have charters. Cities have governing documents of their own. The work of translation matters because states and localities are often where the philosophy can be implemented first, and most concretely.

This document is structured around three questions that any state or local effort must answer before it can proceed:

  • What does the national constitution already establish as a floor that state and local governments are bound to honor, extend, and never contract?

  • What requires specific state constitutional language that the national document does not itself supply?

  • What requires specific municipal charter language for cities, counties, and localities operating within states?

A fourth section addresses a practical question the other three make necessary: what does actual engagement with state constitutional and local charter reform look like, and how does this philosophy enter that process?

The national document sets the floor. The state document builds the first story. The local charter furnishes the room. None of them is the whole building, and none of them is sufficient without the others.

One note on historical context that bears on the framing: state constitutions are in many respects more directly democratic documents than the federal one. Most are longer, more specific, and more frequently amended. Several states have constitutional provisions that go substantially further than the federal document on economic rights, environmental rights, and direct democracy. This is not an accident. State constitutions were often written or rewritten in periods of political mobilization when specific communities had the power to put their priorities directly into the governing document. The tradition of more expansive state constitutionalism is a resource, not a complication.

Part One: What the National Floor Already Establishes

The national constitution's floor provisions bind state and local governments directly. Any state constitution or municipal charter that falls below these provisions is unconstitutional on its face. The work at the state and local level begins with knowing what is already required and building upward from there, never treating the floor as a ceiling.

Equal Protection and Non-Discrimination

The equal protection provision of Article VII applies to every level of government without exception. No state law, no county ordinance, no municipal code may treat any person differently based on race, sex, gender identity, sexual orientation, religion, national origin, disability, or economic status. This is the floor. States may expand the categories of protected characteristics. They may never contract the list the national document provides.

State constitutional practice here has been instructive. Several states added sexual orientation and gender identity to their state equal protection clauses before the federal interpretation of the Fourteenth Amendment reached the same result. The state constitutional addition provided protection in that state that did not yet exist federally. The direction of travel in this framework is always expansion: the state that adds explicit protections for additional categories, for housing status, for immigration status, for weight and appearance, for political affiliation, is doing the work the national floor invites.

Voting Rights

The national constitution establishes the franchise at sixteen, automatic registration, the abolition of the Electoral College, and voting rights for incarcerated people and people under guardianship. These apply to all federal elections and bind state administration of those elections. State constitutions must align their own electoral provisions with these floors for state and local elections.

States have historically been the laboratories of voting reform. Ranked choice voting was adopted in Maine and Alaska before federal legislation addressed it. Automatic voter registration was pioneered at the state level. This framework's voting provisions are floors for federal elections and models for state electoral architecture. A state constitution that extends these provisions to all state and local elections, that adds same-day registration, that creates a state-level public campaign financing system, is building on the floor rather than merely meeting it.

Economic Floor: The Rights of Article VII

The right to adequate food, housing, healthcare, and education established in Article VII is a federal constitutional right enforceable in court. State governments that fall below this floor are in violation of the national constitution. But the federal floor is a minimum threshold. States have broad authority to exceed it: to establish more generous food assistance programs, more expansive housing rights, more comprehensive healthcare coverage, more fully funded public education systems.

The historical pattern is instructive here too. The Medicaid expansion under the Affordable Care Act was optional for states. States that refused it left their residents below the floor the national system offered. In this framework, that option does not exist: the federal floor is a constitutional requirement. But states that build above it, that establish state-level universal healthcare programs, that create state housing authorities with genuine resources, that fund education above the federal equalization baseline, are doing the philosophy's work at the scale where implementation is most immediate.

Direct Democracy Mechanisms

Article I establishes the people as the first branch at the federal level. The initiative, referendum, and recall mechanisms it creates are federal. State constitutions must provide comparable mechanisms for state governance. Twenty-six states currently have some form of citizen initiative process. This framework treats direct democracy not as a supplementary feature but as structurally required: the people who are governed must have direct mechanisms to govern.

The specific parameters of state initiative and referendum processes are state constitutional questions, addressed in Part Two. What the federal floor establishes is the principle: no state constitution is adequate if it provides no mechanism for the people to act directly on the laws that govern them.

Rights That Cannot Be Removed

The rights retained by the people provision of Article VII establishes that rights are not exhausted by what is listed. State constitutions that attempt to enumerate rights as a ceiling, to say these and only these are the rights the people have, are inconsistent with this principle. State constitutional rights provisions must be understood as floors and expansions, never as comprehensive lists that exclude what is not named.

Part Two: What Requires State Constitutional Language

State constitutions are not merely reflections of federal requirements. They govern the structure of state government, the organization of state power, and the specific rights and mechanisms that state residents have against their own state government. Several of the constitution's core provisions require specific state constitutional language that goes beyond what the federal document alone provides.

State-Level Direct Democracy

Federal initiative and referendum provisions govern federal questions. State initiative and referendum provisions govern state law. Every state needs its own specific constitutional language establishing:

  • The petition threshold for a citizen initiative (this framework uses two percent of registered voters at the federal level; state equivalents typically range from four to ten percent, calibrated to the state's voter population)

  • The majority required for passage (simple majority for statutes; supermajority for constitutional amendments, consistent with the federal sixty percent threshold)

  • The subjects excluded from initiative (this framework prohibits initiatives that remove rights from Article VII; state constitutions should prohibit initiatives that contract any right established in the state or federal constitution)

  • The referendum mechanism for reviewing legislative acts before they take effect

  • The recall process for state elected officials, including governors, legislators, and judges where applicable

  • The participatory budgeting provision, adapted to state budget scale

State constitutions have experimented with these provisions extensively. California's initiative process, which requires eight percent of the gubernatorial vote total as signatures, has produced both important expansions of rights and, through the same mechanism, attempted contractions. This framework's approach to this tension is constitutional rights as floors that initiative cannot breach: the initiative that expands rights is always available; the initiative that contracts them is void.

Ohio is a specific case worth attention for Mahoning Valley readers. The 2023 fight over Issue 1, in which the legislature attempted to raise the initiative threshold to sixty percent before a reproductive rights amendment could be voted on, demonstrated both the importance of the initiative mechanism and its vulnerability to manipulation by the legislature it is meant to check. A well-drafted state constitutional provision insulates the initiative threshold itself from legislative revision: it can be changed only by the same supermajority process that would change any other constitutional provision.

State Economic Rights: Building Above the Federal Floor

Several state constitutions already include economic rights provisions that go beyond the federal document. New York's constitution includes a provision requiring the state to provide for the care and support of the needy. Montana's constitution includes an explicit right to a clean and healthful environment. Hawaii's constitution includes a right to a public education. These state-level provisions matter because they are directly enforceable against the state government in state court, without requiring federal constitutional litigation.

A state constitution built on this framework would include explicit enforceable rights to:

  • Housing: not merely as a policy goal but as a justiciable right, with the state obligated to ensure no resident is in chronic housing instability

  • Healthcare: universal coverage through the state's healthcare system, with the state obligated to fill any gap the federal system does not cover

  • Education: fully funded public education from early childhood through post-secondary, with school funding equalized across districts by state law

  • A living income floor: whether through a state minimum wage tied to cost of living, a state earned income tax credit, or a state basic income pilot, the state constitution should specify the mechanism

  • Paid caregiving: state constitutional recognition of care work as economically productive labor, with state law required to establish minimum compensation and benefits for caregiving workers

State Environmental Rights

The Pennsylvania constitution's Article I, Section 27, adopted in 1971, establishes that the people have a right to clean air, pure water, and the preservation of natural, scenic, historic, and aesthetic values of the environment, and that the Commonwealth shall conserve and maintain them for the benefit of all the people including generations yet to come. This provision has been increasingly enforced by Pennsylvania courts to require the state to act on climate, to protect public lands from extraction, and to hold the state accountable for environmental harm.

A state constitution building on this framework would include:

  • An explicit right to a clean and healthful environment for current and future residents

  • Legal standing for state residents to enforce environmental rights in state court

  • A provision establishing the rights of specific natural features, with designated state trustees empowered to act on their behalf

  • A climate obligation tied to specific timelines consistent with scientific consensus, not subject to legislative revision downward

  • An environmental justice provision prohibiting the disproportionate siting of environmental harm in low-income and minority communities

For the Mahoning Valley, an environmental rights provision has specific and immediate relevance. The brownfields left by the steel industry, the ongoing air quality challenges in communities near industrial facilities, the Mahoning River's complicated recovery: all of these are the kind of accumulated environmental harm that a state constitutional provision with teeth could begin to address through litigation and state obligation.

State-Level Wealth and Taxation

Federal tax policy is federal. But states have their own tax systems, and this framework's insistence that concentrated wealth be taxed to fund the floor applies at the state level with full force. A state constitution built on this framework would include:

  • A progressive income tax provision (several states have flat income taxes locked into their constitutions; this framework requires that state constitutions permit, and ideally mandate, progressive structures)

  • A prohibition on regressive taxation structures that shift the burden from wealth to income from labor, from income to consumption

  • A property tax equity provision that prevents the property tax funding of education from producing the zip code lottery this framework identifies as the fundamental injustice of the current system

  • A wealth tax enabling provision, even if the specific rate is left to legislation, establishing the constitutional authority to tax accumulated wealth

State Judiciary and Accountability

The federal constitution's provisions for judicial independence and accountability apply to federal courts. State judicial systems are governed by state constitutional provisions, and they vary enormously. In Ohio, as in many states, Supreme Court justices are elected in partisan elections, creating the same campaign finance dynamics for judicial selection that this framework identifies as corrupting of legislative and executive accountability.

A state constitution building on this framework would include:

  • A merit selection system for state judges with fixed terms and competitive retention review

  • Mandatory recusal requirements for judges with financial interests in cases before them

  • An independent judicial oversight body with genuine authority to investigate and discipline judicial conduct

  • Public financing for judicial elections in states where election is retained

  • An explicit prohibition on the acceptance of gifts, travel, or other benefits by sitting judges

State-Level Historical Reckoning

The constitution's truth and reparative justice provision operates at the federal level. But the specific histories that require reckoning are often state and local histories. The specific decisions about where to put highways through Black neighborhoods, which communities received FHA loans and which were redlined, which counties maintained segregated schools longest: these were state and local decisions as much as federal ones.

A state constitution building on this framework would include:

  • A permanent state truth and historical accountability commission, funded through the state budget, with community governance and democratic oversight

  • Specific acknowledgment of the state's role in specific documented harms, named directly in the constitution rather than left to legislative discretion

  • An ongoing reparative obligation, with the specific mechanisms determined through the community-governed process rather than legislated in advance

  • An education obligation that connects directly to this provision: the state's schools are required to teach the state's actual history, including what the state did

Part Three: What Requires Municipal Charter Language

Cities and counties operate under state-granted authority. Home rule charters give municipalities the maximum authority a state grants to local governments to govern themselves without state legislative approval for every action. A home rule charter is a city's or county's constitution: it establishes the structure of local government, the rights of residents against that government, and the mechanisms through which residents govern directly.

This framework's most immediate implementation is often at the local level. The city that establishes a universal basic income pilot, the county that creates a community land trust authority, the municipality that implements participatory budgeting at meaningful scale: these are not waiting for the federal or state document. They are doing the work in the space the law currently allows, and they are creating the evidence base that state and federal adoption will eventually require.

Home Rule and Its Limits

Home rule authority varies enormously by state. In strong home rule states like Ohio, municipalities have broad authority to govern local affairs without state legislative approval. In Dillon's Rule states, municipalities have only the authority the state legislature explicitly grants. This framework's local implementation operates within whatever home rule authority the state currently provides, while the state constitutional work described in Part Two expands that authority over time.

The immediate practical question for any locality is: what can we do right now, within current state authority, through a home rule charter? The answer is usually more than most local governments attempt. Local charters can establish:

  • Local initiative, referendum, and recall mechanisms more accessible than the state process

  • Local non-discrimination ordinances that exceed state minimums (subject to state preemption, which Part Two's state constitutional work addresses)

  • Local economic floor provisions, including local minimum wages, local paid leave requirements, local anti-wage-theft enforcement

  • Local environmental standards, including local climate action plans with enforceable timelines

  • Local participatory budgeting requirements for defined portions of the local budget

  • Local community land trust authority and affordable housing obligations

  • Local public banking or public financial services provisions

  • Local police accountability structures, including civilian oversight with genuine authority

Local Direct Democracy

This framework's Article I is federal, but its spirit applies at every level. A municipal charter built on this philosophy would include:

  • A citizen initiative process for local ordinances, with a low petition threshold scaled to the local population

  • A mandatory referendum on any ordinance that restructures local voting rights, local governance powers, or that commits the municipality to major long-term financial obligations

  • A recall process for all elected local officials

  • A participatory budgeting process covering at least ten percent of the local discretionary budget, conducted through accessible multilingual in-person and digital processes

  • A citizen oversight board with genuine authority over local administration, not merely advisory standing

Local Economic Floor

Cities and counties are the level of government closest to where the floor either holds or does not. The person who is housing-insecure, food-insecure, or without healthcare is navigating local systems first: the local shelter, the local food bank, the local public hospital. A municipal charter built on this framework would establish:

  • A local right to shelter: the municipality is obligated to ensure that no resident sleeps outside without access to safe shelter, funded through the local budget and state and federal resources

  • A local food security program, operating through the local school system, community centers, and public facilities, available to any resident

  • A local healthcare access obligation, including a public option for primary care through local health departments or community health centers

  • A local living wage requirement for all municipal employees and all contractors doing business with the municipality

  • A local anti-displacement policy, including just-cause eviction requirements, right-to-return provisions for residents displaced by publicly subsidized development, and community benefit agreements for major development projects

Local Environmental Provisions

Municipal environmental provisions have been among the most creative and consequential local governance innovations of the past two decades. Pittsburgh adopted a local environmental rights ordinance modeled on the community rights movement. Several Ohio municipalities have passed resolutions recognizing the rights of local ecosystems, though state courts have sometimes preempted them. A municipal charter built on this framework would include:

  • An explicit local right to a clean and healthful environment for all residents

  • A local climate action plan with enforceable timelines, incorporated into the charter so that it cannot be reversed by a future council majority without a supermajority or a public referendum

  • Local community rights provisions for specific natural features: the local river, the local watershed, the local park system, with designated trustees empowered to act on their behalf

  • A local environmental justice provision prohibiting the siting of polluting facilities in communities already bearing disproportionate environmental burden, with a cumulative impact assessment required for any new permit

  • A local brownfield remediation obligation, funded through a local environmental restoration fund supported by assessments on new development

For the Mahoning Valley specifically, the brownfield provision is not abstract. The region has more brownfield acreage per capita than almost any other metropolitan area in the country. A local charter provision that establishes remediation as an ongoing municipal obligation rather than a project-by-project negotiation with developers would be both constitutionally significant and immediately relevant to community development.

Local Accountability and Transparency

This framework's transparency provisions apply to all levels of government. A municipal charter built on this philosophy would include:

  • Real-time disclosure of all lobbying contacts with elected and appointed officials, in a publicly accessible database

  • Mandatory disclosure of all financial interests of elected and appointed officials, updated annually and available to any resident

  • Campaign contribution caps for local elections, with public financing available to candidates who demonstrate grassroots support through small donations

  • A local inspector general or independent auditor with genuine authority, tenure protections, and the standing to investigate any municipal department or official

  • A community oversight board for local law enforcement with subpoena power, independent investigative authority, and the ability to impose discipline rather than merely recommend it

  • Open meeting requirements more expansive than state law minimums, with genuine accessibility provisions including multilingual interpretation, remote participation, and accessible venues

Local Historical Accountability

Local governments were the direct agents of many of the harms this framework's reparative justice provision addresses. Urban renewal programs that destroyed Black neighborhoods. Highway construction that severed communities of color from economic centers. Local police departments that enforced segregation. Local school boards that maintained separate and unequal systems.

A municipal charter built on this framework would include:

  • A permanent local truth and historical accountability commission, governed by the communities most directly affected, with a budget line in the annual municipal budget

  • A local reparative investment provision, directing a defined percentage of local tax revenue to the communities most directly harmed by documented local government decisions, for a period determined by the democratic process

  • A local curriculum provision, connected to the local school governance structure, requiring that local schools teach the local history honestly, including what the local government did

  • A public memorial and acknowledgment process, governed by affected communities, for the specific losses the local government produced

Part Four: What Engagement with Reform Efforts Actually Looks Like

This section addresses a practical question the other three make necessary: this constitution is a philosophical document with a specific publication strategy. It lives on Substack and as a free PDF. It is not lobbying for a specific piece of legislation, affiliated with a specific political organization, or timed to a specific electoral cycle. The question of how it enters actual reform processes is a real one.

The Landscape of State Constitutional Reform

State constitutional reform is rare and slow by design. Most state constitutions require a supermajority of the legislature plus ratification by the voters to amend. Full conventions, which would allow wholesale revision, are even rarer: most states require legislative referral to trigger a convention, which means the legislature must agree to the process before it begins. The exceptions are states with mandatory periodic convention referendums, where the voters are asked at defined intervals whether they want to call a convention.

The most active current state constitutional reform efforts include:

  • New York, which has a periodic mandatory convention referendum and has seen significant organizing around the question of whether to call one

  • Ohio, which has a history of constitutional initiative campaigns and where the 2023 fight over Issue 1 put the amendment process itself in the public eye

  • Several Western states where environmental rights provisions are being actively litigated and where new provisions are being organized

  • States where reproductive rights campaigns have produced constitutional amendments since 2022, demonstrating that specific single-issue constitutional campaigns can succeed even in difficult political environments

How Philosophical Documents Enter Reform Processes

This constitution is not a lobbying document, but the ideas in it are precisely the kind of intellectual infrastructure that reform movements need and often lack. The gap between 'we want to change this' and 'here is the language and philosophy that would accomplish that change' is where documents like this one do their work.

The specific pathways through which this kind of document enters real reform processes are:

Academic and Legal Infrastructure

Law schools with active constitutional law clinics, think tanks focused on state constitutional law, and academic centers for democracy reform are the institutions that translate philosophical frameworks into draft constitutional language. Organizations like the Brennan Center for Justice, the Center for Constitutional Transitions, and state-specific academic centers regularly publish model constitutional provisions and analyses of state constitutional reform options. This framework's provisions are candidates for this kind of academic translation: the philosophical argument is made, and the legal drafting work would turn it into model language.

Movement Organizations

The organizations most likely to engage with this framework directly are the ones working on specific provisions it addresses. Common Cause and the Brennan Center on voting rights and direct democracy. The National Housing Law Project and housing justice organizations on economic floor provisions. Earthjustice and state environmental law organizations on environmental rights. The ACLU on equal protection and criminal justice. These organizations work with philosophical frameworks when they encounter them, and they are always looking for the intellectual grounding that makes their specific campaigns legible as part of a larger argument.

This framework's distinctive contribution to these conversations is the philosophical grounding it provides for what these organizations advocate. The argument that the economic floor is not charity but the material precondition for the inner life, and that the inner life is not a luxury but the substance of what the constitutional project is for: this is not an argument any of these organizations is currently making, because it requires the philosophical apparatus that this project has been building. The conversation between the philosophy and the movement organizations is the place where the document enters real reform processes.

Local Government Innovation

Local government is where the most immediate implementation happens, and where the barriers are lowest. The city council that adopts a participatory budgeting process does not need a state constitutional amendment. The county that establishes a community land trust authority is working within existing state law. The municipality that creates a local inspector general with genuine authority is exercising home rule power it already has.

This framework is a resource for local elected officials and staff who are trying to do more than their current documents authorize, and for residents who are trying to hold their local governments accountable to a standard more demanding than the minimum the law requires. Local government innovation organizations like the National League of Cities and the National Association of Counties, as well as state-level municipal leagues, are the networks through which ideas about what local charters and ordinances can do circulate among practitioners.

The building continues. The door is open. Come in.

A Rationale for Revision and a Proposed Constitutional Convention

Why a New Constitution

The Constitution of 1787 was a remarkable document for its time. It established a framework for self-governance that was genuinely new in the world, that has proved durable across nearly two and a half centuries, and that contains principles worth preserving. It also contained exclusions built in from the beginning: the three-fifths compromise that counted enslaved people as partial persons for purposes of political representation while denying them any rights that representation was supposed to protect; the assumption that the people doing the governing were propertied white men; the absence of any mechanism for the people to govern directly between elections. Those exclusions were not incidental to the document. They were negotiated into it by the people whose interests they served.

The amendments that followed, the Bill of Rights, the Reconstruction Amendments, the Nineteenth Amendment, the Voting Rights Act's legislative extension of constitutional promises the document had not delivered: these were the work of generations of people insisting that the original exclusions be torn out. That work produced a better document than the one it started with. It did not produce a document adequate to the society it now governs or the challenges that society faces.

The concentration of political power in institutions designed for a nation of four million people now governing about three hundred and forty million. The capture of those institutions by the concentrated economic interests that the founders could not have anticipated at the scale they now operate. The expansion of executive power beyond anything the original document authorized or intended. The electoral system that gives some votes more weight than others based on geography. The absence of any enforceable right to healthcare, housing, education, or a livable environment. The original document has been stretched to cover a world it was not designed for and it shows.

This constitution does not discard what worked. It preserves the separation of powers, the protection of fundamental rights, the federal structure, and the commitment to democratic self-governance that the original document established. It adds what the original document left out: the direct mechanisms for popular sovereignty, the enforceable economic floor, the environmental rights, the explicit equal protection that the original document promised and did not deliver. It corrects what the original document got wrong: the electoral college, the unequal weighting of votes, the absence of term limits for the judiciary, the campaign finance framework that has allowed wealth to purchase political power at scale.

It is offered not as the perfect document but as the better one: the one that takes seriously the promises the original made and did not keep, that addresses the concentrations of power the original did not anticipate, and that builds in the mechanisms for ongoing revision that the original made too difficult.

How Constitutions Change

The original constitution's amendment process requires two-thirds of Congress and three-quarters of states to ratify any change. That threshold was designed to prevent hasty revision and to require genuine consensus before fundamental change. It has also made the document nearly impossible to amend in practice: only twenty-seven amendments have been ratified in two hundred and thirty-five years, and ten of those were the Bill of Rights ratified together in 1791. The practical effect is a document frozen in structures that no longer serve the people they were designed to govern, defended not by consensus but by the veto power of a minority.

This constitution's amendment process is more accessible without being easy. Two paths exist: the congressional path requiring two-thirds of Congress and approval by three-quarters of states measured by population, and the direct path requiring a national initiative approved by sixty percent of voters with at least fifty percent of registered voters participating. The direct path allows the people to amend their own governing document without depending on the willingness of the institutions the amendment might constrain. It requires genuine supermajority support: sixty percent approval is a high threshold that ensures amendments reflect broad consensus rather than temporary majorities.

The constitutional convention is the mechanism for more fundamental revision: the wholesale reconsideration of the document rather than the amendment of specific provisions. The original constitution provides for a convention called by two-thirds of state legislatures, a provision that has never been used and whose procedures are largely unspecified. The absence of specification is itself a problem: a convention called under ambiguous procedures and without clear limits on its scope creates uncertainty about what it could do and whose interests would dominate its proceedings.

The Constitutional Convention: What It Is and When It Is Needed

A constitutional convention is appropriate when the accumulated changes needed exceed what the amendment process can accomplish: when the document needs not revision of specific provisions but reconsideration of its fundamental structure. The history of constitutional change in democratic societies suggests that this need arises roughly generationally: the document that served one era adequately becomes inadequate to the next as the society it governs changes in ways the document's framers could not anticipate.

This constitution does not assume it will be the last word. It assumes it will need to become something different than it is, on a timeline no one can predict, in response to conditions no one can fully foresee. A constitutional convention would be the mechanism for that becoming. It would not be a crisis measure. It would be a democratic tool: the formal process by which the people reconsider the fundamental terms of their self-governance when those terms need more than amendment.

The draft constitution does not yet include a convention clause. This essay proposes one, to be added to Article VI, built on the following principles.

Who Calls It

Under this proposal, a constitutional convention could be called by any of three mechanisms: a petition signed by five percent of registered voters triggering a national referendum in which sixty percent approve the calling of a convention; a two-thirds vote of Congress submitting the question to a national referendum with the same sixty percent threshold; or the determination by the independent judiciary that a fundamental constitutional question has arisen that the existing document cannot adequately resolve, submitted to a national referendum with the same threshold. The multiple paths would ensure that the convention could be called by popular initiative, by legislative consensus, or in response to genuine constitutional crisis, without any single institution having unilateral power to call or block it.

Who Participates

The proposed convention would be a democratic body, not a body of experts. It would be composed of delegates selected through a process that combines election and sortition: some delegates are elected from geographic districts using the same ranked choice voting system that governs other elections; others are selected by stratified random sample from the registered voter population, ensuring that the convention reflects the demographic composition of the country rather than only the people most motivated and resourced to seek elected positions. Legal scholars, historians, and subject matter experts would participate as advisors to the convention rather than as delegates with votes. The people govern. The experts inform.

The convention would be required to conduct its deliberations in public, with full records available to every citizen. It would be required to receive testimony from the communities most directly affected by the provisions under consideration. It would be required to produce plain-language summaries of every proposed change accessible to the full voting population. The convention that deliberates in private, that excludes affected communities, or that produces documents readable only by lawyers is not doing democratic work. It is doing the work of the people with the resources to participate in opaque processes, which is what the original convention did.

What It Can and Cannot Do

The convention could reconsider any provision of this constitution and propose changes to the full voting population for ratification. It could propose an entirely new document. It could propose targeted revisions to specific articles. The scope of what it considers would be determined by the mandate under which it was called: a convention called to address a specific constitutional question has a specific mandate; a convention called for general revision has a broader one.

What the convention could not do is remove the floor. The rights established in Article VII, the direct democracy mechanisms established in Article I, and the equal protection principle that runs through the entire document are not subject to removal by any convention or any amendment. They may be expanded. They may never be contracted. The floor is permanent. A convention that proposed to remove it would have exceeded its mandate, and its proposals would be void.

This constraint is not a limitation on democracy. It is democracy's protection of itself. The history of democratic backsliding in the twentieth and twenty-first centuries is largely the history of democratic majorities voting away the rights of minorities, of temporary majorities using the mechanisms of democracy to entrench their own power and exclude their opponents. The floor provisions are the safeguard against that history repeating. They are what the people have agreed they will not do to each other regardless of what any majority at any moment wants.

Ratification

Proposals from the convention would be submitted to the full voting population for ratification. Ratification would require sixty percent approval with at least fifty percent of registered voters participating. The threshold would be the same as for constitutional amendments by initiative: high enough to require genuine broad consensus, low enough to be achievable when consensus exists. A proposal that cannot achieve sixty percent approval has not achieved the consensus required to change the fundamental terms of self-governance. It would return to the democratic process for further deliberation.

The ratification campaign would be subject to the same campaign finance provisions as all other electoral contests. The side with the most money does not get to drown out the side with less. The public media system is obligated to provide full and fair coverage of the ratification debate, including the perspectives of communities most directly affected by the proposed changes. The voter who goes to the ratification referendum would have access to the full text of the proposed changes, independent assessments of their likely consequences, and plain-language summaries prepared without advocacy for either side.

Why Revision Is Integrity

The document that cannot be revised is not a strong document. It is a frozen one: unable to respond to what it did not anticipate, defending its own inadequacies as though they were features rather than failures. The constitution that acknowledges its own incompleteness and builds in the mechanisms for honest revision is more trustworthy than the one that presents itself as finished.

This constitution is not finished. It is the best map its writers could draw of the territory they are trying to reach. The territory will keep revealing itself to be larger than the map accounts for. New conditions will arise that the map does not address. Provisions that seemed adequate will prove inadequate in application. Communities whose experiences the writers could not fully see will identify what the document has missed.

A constitutional convention would be the formal mechanism for responding to that ongoing revelation. Calling one would not be a sign that the document has failed. It would be the sign that the democracy is working: that the people retain genuine authority over the fundamental terms of their own governance, that they can use that authority when the document needs to become something different than it is, and that the work of building a more just society does not end with the ratification of any document however carefully written.

The sentence has not ended. The amendment is always possible. The convention, once added, would always be available. The people are always the government.

Preamble

We, the people of this nation (all of us, without exception of race, sex, gender identity, sexual orientation, national origin, religion, disability, class, or condition of birth) establish this Constitution. We do so not to hand our power to representatives and trust that it will be used wisely. We do so to hold that power ourselves, delegating it where delegation is practical and reclaiming it where it is not. Government answers to the people directly. This document is how we make that true.

Article I

The People Are the First Branch

Before any structure of elected government, the people hold sovereign legislative power directly. This is not a metaphor. It is a mechanism.

National initiative: Any proposed law or constitutional amendment may be placed before the full voting public by petition. A petition signed by two percent of registered voters triggers a national referendum. A majority vote enacts the measure into law, with the same force as any act of Congress. Constitutional amendments by initiative require sixty percent approval.

National referendum: Congress must submit any law that significantly restructures voting rights, civil rights protections, or the powers of government itself to a public referendum before it takes effect. The people confirm or reject it. A simple majority decides.

Popular recall: Any elected federal official may be removed from office before their term ends by a recall petition signed by ten percent of voters in their district or state, followed by a recall election. The replacement is elected simultaneously on the same ballot, so no office is vacant and no appointment fills a democratic seat.

Participatory budgeting: A fixed percentage of the federal discretionary budget, no less than five percent, is allocated annually through direct public vote. Citizens propose, deliberate, and decide how these funds are spent. The process is open, multilingual, accessible to all, and conducted both digitally and in person.

On manipulation: Direct democracy is only as good as the information available to voters. Corporate spending, foreign interference, and coordinated disinformation campaigns in referendum contests are treated as election fraud. Independent public media, funded by the government and free to report without government direction, is a constitutional obligation, not an option. That public media is further obligated to represent the full plurality of human voices and experiences, including those historically excluded from the version of reality held by those already in power, rather than to reproduce a single dominant version of public reality. Democracy requires a commons of expression adequate to the actual diversity of the people it serves.

On civic capacity: The ability to participate meaningfully in self-governance is a skill, not an instinct. The government is obligated to support civic education at every level: education in the practice of thinking through disagreements together, in holding competing perspectives simultaneously, in recognizing the difference between the assumptions and stories we take for granted and the versions held by others. Citizens who can witness, who can stay in the room with complexity without demanding premature resolution, are the foundation of functional democracy. That capacity must be cultivated, not assumed.

Article II

The Legislature: Making Law on Behalf of the People

Congress makes law between elections and referendums. It has two chambers. The House of Representatives seats are allocated by full population, with every person counted as a whole person. Senate seats are allocated by state population; no state may block the national majority simply because it is small.

Members of Congress are elected by ranked-choice voting in districts that elect more than one representative, so that minority communities and third parties achieve meaningful representation proportional to their numbers. No gerrymandering: district maps are drawn by independent commissions, with members drawn equally from all parties and from citizens who belong to none, subject to public comment and judicial review.

Any law passed by Congress may be challenged by popular referendum within two years of passage. A petition of three percent of registered voters triggers the vote. If the public rejects the law, it is repealed. This is the legislative check that the original Constitution never provided: the people may undo what their representatives do.

On money: Campaign contributions are capped and publicly disclosed in real time. No private entity may spend more than a citizen on elections. Elected officials may not receive income from private sources during their term. Any meeting or communication between a lobbyist and an elected official is a matter of public record within 48 hours.

Article III

The Executive: Carrying Out What the People Decide

The President executes law. The President does not make law, does not suspend law, and does not stand above it. The President is elected by national popular vote, every vote weighted equally regardless of geography.

The President's financial records, tax returns, and any situation where the President's personal finances could benefit from a government decision must be publicly disclosed. No person may serve as President while holding private financial stakes in government contracts, industries overseen by the federal government, or foreign governments. Violation is automatic grounds for removal.

The President may not pardon themselves, members of their administration, or family members for acts committed while in office or related to their official duties. Emergency powers are limited to ninety days without being renewed by Congress and are subject to immediate judicial review. The people may trigger a recall referendum against the President by petition of fifteen percent of registered voters.

Article IV

The Judiciary: Protecting Rights Against Majorities

The courts interpret this Constitution. Their specific function is to protect the rights listed in Article VII, especially when those rights are threatened by popular majorities. Direct democracy does not override fundamental rights. The people may not vote away another group's personhood, equal protection, or dignity.

Supreme Court justices serve fixed eighteen-year terms, with one appointment every two years, so that no single administration appoints too many justices. Justices may not accept gifts, travel, financial benefits, or any compensation from anyone with a case before the court. A justice must step aside from any case where they have a personal or financial interest. Failure to step aside when required is grounds for removal by a two-thirds vote of the full Congress, confirmed by public referendum.

Judicial nominees are confirmed by a public hearing process that is fully transparent, with written records available to every citizen, followed by Senate confirmation by a majority vote.

Article V

States, Localities, and the Federal Structure

States govern themselves in matters of local concern. Cities and localities hold genuine governing authority over local matters; state governments may not strip local governments of their power to respond to their own communities' needs.

No state may deny any person the rights guaranteed in Article VII. The rights of people do not end at state lines. States may expand rights beyond the minimum rights this Constitution guarantees; they may never contract below it.

Direct democracy mechanisms apply at every level of government. States and localities are encouraged to develop their own initiative, referendum, and recall systems consistent with this Constitution's principles. Federal funding supports the tools and systems people need to participate in democracy, including internet access, polling locations, and civic education, so that participation is not limited by wealth, geography, or access to technology.

Article VI

Amending This Constitution

This Constitution can be changed by two paths: the traditional path, requiring two-thirds of Congress and approval by three-quarters of states measured by population; or the direct path, requiring a national initiative approved by sixty percent of voters in a national referendum, with at least fifty percent of registered voters participating.

No amendment may remove the rights guaranteed in Article VII, strip the vote from any citizen, or eliminate the direct democracy mechanisms established in Article I. These are the floor. They may be expanded but never removed.

Article VII

The Rights of All People: These Are the Floor, Not the Ceiling

Equal protection: Every person is equal before the law. No law may treat people differently based on race, sex, gender identity, sexual orientation, religion, national origin, disability, or economic status.

The vote: Every person sixteen or older votes, with full and equal standing. Voting is a right, not a privilege. It may not be restricted by criminal record, immigration status, cognitive or physical disability, guardianship status, ID requirement designed to exclude, or any administrative barrier. A person under guardianship or held in prison keeps the full right to vote. Registration is automatic at sixteen. Election Day is a national holiday. The Electoral College is abolished.

Free expression: Speech, press, religion, and peaceful assembly are protected. No government may suppress dissent, restrict journalism, or establish any religion as official.

Due process: No person may be imprisoned, punished, or deprived of property without fair legal process. This applies to every person on this soil, regardless of citizenship status.

Economic floor: Every person has the right to adequate food, housing, healthcare, and education. The government is obligated to ensure no one falls below a dignified minimum. This floor is not charity. It is the condition of possibility for everything else in this Constitution. A person whose entire capacity is consumed by survival cannot participate in self-governance, cannot develop the plural self the culture requires, cannot grieve honestly, cannot witness, cannot build. The economic floor is the material prerequisite for the kind of citizenship this Constitution envisions. Courts may enforce it.

Education: Every person has the right to public education from early childhood through post-secondary or vocational training, free at the point of use. Public education is the shared space where a plural society learns to be in a room together, and private schools that select their students by wealth, religion, or any other criterion of exclusion are inconsistent with this principle. Funding is equalized across all public schools, and federal funding is obligated to close resource gaps wherever they exist, so that the accident of zip code does not determine the quality of education a child receives. Students are entitled to the complete record of human history and experience, including the histories of communities historically excluded and the uncomfortable parts. Public education is obligated to develop the capacity for complexity: for holding multiple perspectives at once and staying in the room with difficulty rather than demanding its premature resolution. Education that produces compliance rather than witnesses is a constitutional failure.

Bodily autonomy: Every person has sovereignty over their own body. Medical decisions belong to the individual. The state may not compel pregnancy, compel medical treatment, or police private consensual conduct.

Environmental right: Every person has the right to clean air, clean water, and a livable climate. Future generations hold this right as well. The natural world carries what human civilization produces; its capacity to carry is not unlimited and its degradation is not reversible on human timescales. The government is obligated to act; inaction in the face of documented environmental harm is a constitutional violation.

Privacy: Every person has the right to privacy in their communications, data, and personal life. Surveillance requires a judicial warrant. No government or corporation may collect personal data without informed, revocable consent.

Freedom from caste: No hereditary privilege, title, or structural caste system may be recognized or enforced by law. Wealth may not be used to purchase rights unavailable to others. Equal justice is not a metaphor.

Freedom from cruel punishment: No person may be subjected to cruel, degrading, or disproportionate punishment. The state is obligated to witness the suffering it produces: to see it, name it, and be accountable for it. Solitary confinement beyond seventy-two hours, the death penalty, and conditions of incarceration that destroy physical or psychological health are constitutional violations. The carceral system is not outside the frame of equal protection. Every person held by the state retains full human dignity. Punishment that requires looking away from the person being punished is not justice. It is the demand that suffering be made invisible so that the system producing it need not reckon with itself.

Historical repair: This nation was built on losses that have not resolved. The theft of indigenous land, the centuries of enslaved labor, the systematic exclusion of women, queer people, disabled people, and immigrants from the promises this nation made about itself: these are not events in the past. They are conditions in the present, carried forward in bodies, in communities, in landscapes, and in the accumulated structures of who has access to what. The Earth holds what the political system has demanded be called finished. The people most directly descended from these losses cannot be asked to perform a recovery they have not experienced. The federal government is obligated to establish and fund a permanent truth commission and a process of acknowledgment and repair for historical wrongs: not as punishment, not as the final word, but as the honest institutional acknowledgment that the grief is cumulative, the carrying is collective, and the work of reckoning does not end on a deadline set by law. That process must be ongoing, multilingual, community-rooted, and subject to direct democratic oversight.

Rights retained by the people: The rights listed in this Constitution do not constitute an exhaustive list. The people retain all rights not explicitly prohibited by this document.
