No branch of government may use the absence of explicit listing to deny or disparage a right held by the people. Rights are not granted by constitutions: they are recognized by them, and recognition is always subject to expansion as the people's understanding of their own dignity deepens.

Each right listed above is a floor. Companion documents explain how each right is put into practice in full.

Article VIII

Citizenship and Belonging

Citizenship is established by three paths: birthright, for every person born on this soil regardless of the status of their parents; applying for citizenship, through a process that is fair, accessible, and not designed as an obstacle course; and long-term residency, for every person who has lived here, worked here, raised families here, and been subject to the laws here for a defined continuous period. Achieving a legal status through bureaucratic process is not the measure of belonging. Presence and subjection to law are the measure of belonging.

Voting rights extend to all residents subject to the laws of this nation, not citizens alone. The person who pays taxes here, who sends children to schools here, who is arrested under laws made here, has a stake in who makes those laws. The demand that people be governed without voice is the original grievance of this nation's founding and it has never been fully resolved. It is resolved here.

The asylum and immigration system is redesigned around the principle that people do not abandon their homes and communities without cause, and that the causes are knowable and often traceable to the decisions of this government. The nation that destabilized the country you fled has an obligation toward you that exceeds the current framework. Processing is humane, timely, and conducted with the full recognition that the person seeking entry is a full person with a history and a life, not a category to be sorted. No person is held in detention under conditions that violate the freedom from cruel punishment provision of Article VII.

Indigenous peoples' relationship to this land precedes the nation that now administers it. Tribal sovereignty is a constitutional fact, not a federal concession. Treaties are honored. The long-term residency path to citizenship does not apply to people whose nations predate this one: they are not immigrants on their own land.

Article IX

Security and the Common Defense

Security means the protection of people's actual ability to live full lives: to have food, housing, healthcare, education, bodily autonomy, environmental safety, and freedom from violence. It does not mean the extension of military or economic dominance over other countries. The defense of this nation is the defense of its people and their rights, not the defense of the interests of its most powerful institutions.

The use of military force requires a declaration of war by Congress. No President may commit forces to sustained combat without approval from Congress. Emergency deployments are permitted for up to thirty days without Congressional approval, after which Congress must vote to authorize the continuation of the deployment or it ends. The people may not be taken to war by executive decision alone. The decision to use violence in the name of the nation belongs to the nation's representatives, accountable to the nation's people, and subject to the nation's referendum mechanisms when the people demand it.

Companies that profit from military contracts may not purchase influence over security policy. Contracts, lobbying contacts, and financial relationships between these companies and elected or appointed officials are subject to the full transparency provisions of this Constitution. The movement of military leaders directly into employment with defense companies is a conflict of interest subject to the same prohibitions as any other. Security policy is made in the public interest, not the interest of the industry that profits from its expansion.

Peace-building, conflict prevention, and the systems and institutions that support negotiation and peaceful resolution of conflict are constitutional obligations, funded at a ratio defined by law relative to military spending. A nation that invests only in the capacity for violence and not in the conditions that make violence unnecessary has chosen a particular construction of how the world works and called it realism. It is not realism. It is a system that produces the very conflicts it claims to prepare for. Security spending that comes at the cost of the economic floor, the environmental right, or the education provision is itself a security failure: a population without a floor is not a secure population regardless of the force deployed in its name.

Existing military capacity is progressively redirected toward the obligations this Constitution has already established: engineering and infrastructure toward the environmental right and climate resilience; the military's ability to move people and supplies toward disaster response and public health; research and development toward the shift to clean and renewable energy; medical infrastructure toward the universal healthcare obligation. Conversion is not abolition. It is the redirection of enormous existing capacity toward the purposes a government of the people actually requires.

Article X

The Economic System: What It Is For

The economy exists to serve the people. The people do not exist to serve the economy. How we structure the economy is a political choice that democracy can change, not a natural law exempt from democratic accountability. The market price is not the measure of value. Care, community, the natural world, and the interior life have value that the market does not count and cannot count. The failure to count them is a political choice, not an objective fact about what has value.

No person's access to the economic floor established in Article VII may be contingent on what the market currently values or demands. The person who is grieving, caring for another, disabled, young, old, or simply not currently demanded by the market retains full access to food, housing, healthcare, and education. Survival is not a reward for productivity. It is the condition of possibility for everything else.

The care economy is counted. The work of raising children, tending the sick, maintaining households and communities, and sustaining the relationships on which all other economic activity depends is recognized as productive work in every measure of national wellbeing. An economy that does not count this work has decided in advance whose labor matters. That decision is reversed here.

Wealth beyond what any person can meaningfully use is taxed at rates that fund the floor for everyone. The accumulation of that wealth was only possible because of the collective infrastructure: the educated workforce, the legal system, the public research, the stable society that the floor provision maintains. Taxation of concentrated wealth is not redistribution. It is the return of what the commons made possible to the commons that made it possible.

Public options exist in every domain where the market systematically fails to serve the floor: banking, healthcare, housing, energy, broadband, and any other domain where taking profit from people's basic needs produces outcomes inconsistent with the rights listed in Article VII. The public option does not prohibit private enterprise. It ensures that private enterprise competes on the basis of genuine value rather than on the basis of having no competition.

Businesses owned and governed by their workers are supported by law and by public investment as alternatives to the concentration of ownership that produces concentrated power. The person who works in a place has a stake in how that place is governed that the current system does not count. It is counted here.

National wellbeing is measured by whether people can live full lives: by the health of the floor, the quality of the air and water, the condition of care relationships, the time available for rest and community, the distribution of security across the full population. Growth in the market price of things is not the measure. The good economy is the one that operates within the floor and the limits of what the natural world can sustain simultaneously, in the space where human life can actually be lived.

Article XI

What This Constitution Is For

This document exists because power concentrates. It exists because majorities have harmed minorities. It exists because the original promises of this nation were written with exclusions built in, and those exclusions had to be torn out over generations at enormous cost in blood and suffering. We do not pretend that writing a better document ends that struggle. We write it anyway, because the struggle needs a map.

Every provision here is meant to be used. Rights that cannot be enforced are decoration. Democracy that cannot reach actual decisions is theater. The people are not the audience. The people are the government.

This Constitution is not finished. No constitution ever is. The amendment process exists because revision is integrity, not failure. What this document builds cannot be torn down. What it has not yet imagined can always be added. The floor is permanent. The ceiling keeps rising.

This Constitution implies a set of companion documents that do the work it can only gesture at: on patriarchy, sexism, and misogyny; women, children, and the unpaid economy; education; the abolition of private schooling; the economic system; voting and electoral systems; citizenship and immigration; healthcare; historical grief and reparative justice; criminal justice and the carceral system; environmental rights and obligations; media and information; and security and the common defense. Those documents follow.

Closing note

This document is written to be readable by the people it governs, including the sixteen-year-olds who hold full voting rights under it. Companion documents and civic education materials exist to support full engagement with every provision. No one is expected to arrive at this document already knowing everything it contains. That is what the education obligation is for.
floor-14-criminal-justice-and-the-carcer:
Criminal Justice and the Carceral System

← Historical Grief and Reparative Justice · The Floor and the Framework · Environmental Rights and Obligations →

Accountability, Harm, and What Comes After

A Companion Document to the Constitution

The Philosophical Foundation

The American carceral system is the largest in the world by total incarcerated population and among the highest in the world in its rate of incarceration per capita, the length of its sentences, and the scope of its criminal code. It is also the most racially stratified, the most expensive relative to its outcomes, and the least effective by its own stated measures of reducing harm and producing public safety. These are not accidental features of a system that is otherwise working. They are the predictable outcomes of a system built to serve purposes other than the ones it claims.

The carceral system presents itself as the natural response to crime, as simply what happens when people break the law, as the inevitable mechanism of a society that takes harm seriously. It is a construction. The decision to respond to harm with caging was made by specific people at specific historical moments for specific reasons, many of them having nothing to do with the reduction of harm and everything to do with the control of specific populations. The construction of crime itself, the decision about which harmful acts are crimes and which are not, which harms are prosecuted aggressively and which are treated as the cost of doing business, encodes the interests of the people who built the criminal code.

A system that requires the suffering it produces to be invisible cannot be a just system. The person in solitary confinement, the person in the immigration detention facility, the person serving a mandatory minimum sentence for a nonviolent drug offense, the person who cannot afford bail and sits in pretrial detention losing their job and housing while awaiting a trial that may acquit them: all of these are people whose suffering the system is designed to make invisible. The demand that the suffering be witnessed, named, and made the basis of accountability is not soft on crime. It is the precondition for any system that is actually oriented toward reducing harm.

What the System Is Actually Doing

The Racial Construction of Crime

The United States incarcerates Black people at five times the rate of white people. This disparity cannot be explained by differential rates of harmful behavior. The research is consistent: white and Black people use drugs at similar rates and commit similar rates of many offenses, but are policed, arrested, prosecuted, convicted, and sentenced at dramatically different rates. The disparity is produced at every stage of the system, from the deployment of police resources toward Black communities and away from white ones, to the charging decisions of prosecutors, to the bail decisions of judges, to the sentencing decisions that produce longer terms for Black defendants than for white defendants convicted of identical offenses.

This is accumulated loss built into the foundation of this nation, reproduced through the criminal legal system after direct forms of racial exclusion became constitutionally impermissible. The Black Codes after Reconstruction that recriminalized Black freedom. The convict leasing system that restored forced labor under the Thirteenth Amendment's exception for punishment of crime. The war on drugs that targeted crack cocaine, prevalent in Black communities, with penalties one hundred times harsher than powder cocaine, prevalent in white ones. The mass incarceration that followed, which by the 1990s had produced a rate of Black incarceration that exceeded apartheid South Africa. This is not history. It is the present condition of the system. The construction has been maintained because it continues to serve the interests it was built to serve.

What Incarceration Does and Does Not Do

The research on incarceration as a mechanism for reducing crime is extensive and largely consistent: it does not work the way the system claims. Incarceration has a modest incapacitation effect: the person who is caged cannot commit further offenses in the community while caged. But the deterrence effect, the idea that the threat of incarceration prevents people from committing offenses, is weak and highly conditional. People who commit crimes generally do not engage in the expected utility calculation that deterrence theory requires. They act under conditions of stress, poverty, addiction, trauma, and immediate circumstance that make the distant threat of incarceration less relevant than the immediate conditions producing the behavior.

The recidivism rate, the rate at which people who have been incarcerated commit further offenses after release, is consistently around two-thirds within three years. This means that two-thirds of the time, incarceration has not changed the conditions that produced the original behavior. The conditions that produce criminal behavior are well documented: poverty, trauma, addiction, educational failure, housing instability, lack of legitimate economic opportunity, community disinvestment. Incarceration does not address any of these conditions. It often makes them worse: the incarcerated person loses employment, housing, family connections, and any economic stability they had, and emerges into the same or worse conditions than the ones that produced the original behavior, now additionally burdened with a criminal record that forecloses many legitimate opportunities.

The communities from which incarcerated people are drawn and to which they return experience mass incarceration as a form of community devastation: the removal of working-age adults, the disruption of family structures, the economic contraction, the trauma transmitted to children who have a parent incarcerated. The research on children of incarcerated parents documents elevated rates of behavioral problems, academic failure, poverty, and eventual incarceration. The carceral system reproduces the conditions that produce it. This is not a failure of the system. It is the system working as designed.

What Accountability Without Caging Looks Like

Restorative Justice

Restorative justice is a framework for responding to harm that asks different questions than the current system. Not: what rule was broken and what punishment does the rule prescribe? But: who was harmed, what do they need, who is responsible for the harm, and what can the person responsible do to make it right? The framework is not new. It draws on indigenous practices of conflict resolution from cultures around the world, on community accountability traditions that predate the modern criminal legal system, on the understanding that harm is fundamentally relational and that the repair of harm requires addressing the relationship rather than simply punishing the individual.

The research on restorative justice outcomes is consistently more positive than the research on incarceration outcomes: higher rates of victim satisfaction, lower rates of reoffense, lower costs, and the repair of community relationships that the adversarial criminal process damages. Restorative practices have been implemented in schools, communities, and criminal legal systems at various scales, with results that challenge the assumption that punishment is the only serious response to harm.

Restorative justice requires that the person who caused harm see the full weight of what they caused, that the person who was harmed be seen and heard by the process rather than processed as a complainant, and that the community affected by the harm be present to the repair rather than excluded from it. The criminal trial as currently constructed does none of these things reliably. The victim is a witness for the prosecution, not a participant in determining what repair looks like. The person who caused harm sits through a process in which the harm they caused is often less visible than the procedural maneuvering around it. The community is the gallery.

Rehabilitation as a Constitutional Obligation

If the state takes a person's liberty, the state assumes an obligation to that person. The obligation is not only to hold them securely. It is to return them, to the extent possible, to the conditions that enable full participation in community life. This means education: the right to educational programs during incarceration, including post-secondary education, the ban on which was a policy choice with no penological justification and clear negative effects on recidivism. It means addiction treatment: the majority of people incarcerated for drug offenses are people with substance use disorders, and incarceration without treatment does not address the disorder, only removes the person from the community temporarily.

It means mental health treatment: the deinstitutionalization movement of the 1970s closed psychiatric hospitals without building the community mental health infrastructure that was supposed to replace them, and the resulting gap was filled by the criminal legal system, which is now the largest provider of mental health services in the country through jails and prisons that are profoundly ill-equipped to provide them. The person with a serious mental illness who cycles through emergency rooms, jails, and the street is not being served by any system. They are being processed by a system that has no idea what to do with them and responds with the only tool it has: incarceration.

It means housing: the person released from incarceration into homelessness is being released into the conditions most directly associated with reincarceration. The connection between housing instability and criminal legal involvement is one of the most thoroughly documented relationships in criminology. Housing first policies, which provide stable housing without preconditions to people with histories of homelessness and criminal legal involvement, produce consistent reductions in criminal legal involvement. The investment in housing is an investment in public safety that outperforms incarceration by every measure.

Solitary Confinement

Solitary confinement is torture. The research on the psychological effects of isolation is unambiguous: prolonged solitary confinement produces psychosis, severe depression, self-harm, and permanent psychological damage in people who had no prior mental health history. The United Nations Standard Minimum Rules for the Treatment of Prisoners, the Nelson Mandela Rules, define solitary confinement beyond fifteen days as cruel, inhuman, or degrading treatment. The United States routinely holds people in solitary for months, years, and in some cases decades.

This constitution's freedom from cruel punishment provision bans solitary confinement beyond seventy-two hours. The enforcement of that ban requires independent oversight of correctional facilities, regular inspection by bodies with genuine authority to impose consequences, and the standing of incarcerated people to bring constitutional challenges without the procedural barriers the Prison Litigation Reform Act currently imposes. Incarcerated people in the United States have been systematically stripped of the legal mechanisms to report what is done to them. This constitution restores those mechanisms.

The Death Penalty

The death penalty is a constitutional violation under the freedom from cruel punishment provision. It is also a demonstrated failure by the system's own standards: it does not deter, it is applied with documented racial disparity, it has produced the execution of innocent people at a rate the Innocence Project has documented through DNA exonerations, and it costs more than life imprisonment when the full cost of the appellate process is included. The argument for its retention is not penological. It is retributive: the belief that some offenses require death as the appropriate response.

The demand that the person who caused harm suffer the maximum possible suffering is not the same as the demand that the harm be witnessed and repaired. Retribution is the attempt to resolve grief over a loss by producing an equivalent loss. It does not resolve the grief. The research on victims' families and the death penalty consistently shows that the execution does not produce the closure it promises. The loss remains. What the witness pillar asks instead is that we stay in the room with the grief rather than seeking its resolution through further harm.

Policing

Policing as currently practiced is the enforcement arm of the construction the criminal legal system maintains. The deployment of police resources is a political choice: the decision to heavily police some communities and not others, to prioritize some offenses and not others, to treat some encounters as opportunities for assistance and others as opportunities for control, reflects the values and interests of the people making the deployment decisions. Those decisions have consistently reflected the interests of the people with political power and subordinated the interests of the people without it.

The transformation of policing required by this document is not the abolition of any community safety infrastructure. It is the redefinition of what community safety requires and who is best positioned to provide it. The mental health crisis is not a policing problem: it requires mental health professionals. The domestic dispute is not reliably a policing problem: it requires social workers and the infrastructure of domestic violence response. The person in a drug crisis is not a policing problem: they require medical intervention. The call for service that requires an armed officer with the authority to use lethal force is a subset of the calls that currently receive that response. The appropriate response to the full range of community safety needs is a full range of community safety infrastructure, of which armed policing is one component deployed in the specific circumstances where it is actually appropriate.

Accountability for police violence requires genuine consequences. The qualified immunity doctrine, which shields officers from civil liability for constitutional violations unless the specific violation has been previously clearly established in court, is a political choice presented as legal doctrine: the protection of the dominant enforcement apparatus from the accountability mechanisms that apply to everyone else. It is repealed. Officers who use force are accountable to the same legal standards as anyone else who uses force. Departments whose patterns of conduct produce systematic constitutional violations are subject to federal oversight and intervention. The person harmed by police violence has the same legal standing to seek remedy as any other person harmed by any other person.

The Transition

The transition from the current carceral system to the one this document describes is the longest and most politically difficult of all the transitions the companion documents require. The carceral system has enormous institutional inertia, a powerful political economy built around its continuation, and decades of public messaging that has constructed the incarcerated person as the appropriate object of punishment rather than as a person whose circumstances the system has failed to address.

The transition requires the immediate implementation of the constitutional prohibitions: the end of solitary confinement beyond seventy-two hours, the abolition of the death penalty, the restoration of voting rights for incarcerated people. These are not gradual. They are constitutional requirements that take effect immediately.

The longer-term transition requires building the infrastructure the current system lacks: the mental health system, the addiction treatment system, the housing system, the educational and economic opportunity system that addresses the conditions producing harm rather than warehousing the people who act on them. It requires the scaling of restorative justice practices. It requires the rebuilding of communities that have been devastated by mass incarceration over decades. It requires the truth and reparative justice process of Article VII applied specifically to the history of racial construction in the criminal legal system.

None of this happens overnight. All of it is possible.
floor-04-a-note-on-these-documents:
A Note on These Documents

← Constitution of the United States, Revised Draft · The Floor and the Framework · Patriarchy, Sexism, and Misogyny →

An Introduction to the Companion Document Series

The companion documents that follow are the first attempt to describe the territory the constitution points toward. They explain how the rights established in the constitution are put into practice, what the specific provisions mean in specific domains, and what the transition from the current system to the one the constitution envisions would require.

They are not the final word on any of the subjects they address. They were written by people with particular histories, particular blind spots, and particular limits on what they can see from where they stand. Every document in this series will have missed something. Some of what they missed will be obvious to people whose experiences are different from the ones that shaped the writing. Some of it will only become visible as the society these documents are trying to build comes into fuller view. That is the honest condition of any attempt to describe a more just world from inside the unjust one.

These documents are offered as starting points. They are written to be used: argued with, extended, revised, and replaced as the democratic work of building the society they describe proceeds. The provisions in each document are grounded in the best available evidence and the clearest philosophical framework the writers could bring to them. They are not grounded in certainty that every provision is correct or complete. Where they are wrong, they should be corrected. Where they are incomplete, they should be extended. Where they have missed an entire dimension of a problem, that dimension should be added.

The people most directly affected by each domain these documents address are the people best positioned to identify what the documents have missed. The companion document on historical grief was not written by the indigenous communities whose history it describes or the Black communities whose losses it names. The companion document on patriarchy was not written by every woman whose experience of misogyny differs from the experiences the document was able to see. The companion document on criminal justice was not written by the people most directly affected by mass incarceration. These documents are not substitutes for the voices of the people they are about. They are an attempt to build a framework adequate to receive those voices and act on what they say.

The series will grow. Domains not yet addressed will need their own documents. Provisions in existing documents will need revision as implementation reveals what the writing could not anticipate. The spirit of the amendment process in Article VI applies to these documents too.

The building continues. The door is open. Come in.
floor-08-the-abolition-of-private-school:
The Abolition of Private Schooling

← Education · The Floor and the Framework · The Economic System →

Why Separate Is Never Equal and What Comes After

A Companion Document to the Constitution

The Philosophical Foundation

Private schooling allows families with money to choose who their children go to school with. When parents choose a private school, they are often choosing a school where the student body is economically and racially similar. Children in those schools grow up without sustained contact with people whose lives look very different from their own.

This matters educationally. One of the core purposes of education, in the framework this constitution is built on, is developing the capacity to be genuinely present to other people: to understand their experiences, to take their lives seriously, to think and reason alongside them. That capacity does not develop in a school from which difference has been screened out by tuition. A child who has never been required to share a classroom with someone from a radically different background has missed something that no amount of academic preparation can substitute for.

The other side of the sorting causes its own harm. The child in the underfunded public school receives a clear message from the structure of the system: the families who could afford to leave have left, and their departure has taken resources, political attention, and social investment with them. That is not a neutral fact. It tells children something about whose education the society considers worth funding.

Private schooling is not incidentally connected to class reproduction. It is one of its primary mechanisms. The networks, the expectations, the ease in professional and social settings where power is exercised: these are transmitted through the experience of being educated alongside other children whose families have resources. The abolition of private schooling is an argument about what education is for and who it is for.

The History

Private Schools and Segregation

The modern American private school system cannot be understood outside its relationship to school desegregation. After the Supreme Court's 1954 decision in Brown v. Board of Education required the integration of public schools, many communities, particularly in the South, responded by creating private schools that could maintain racial separation after the law required public schools to integrate. The White Citizens' Councils that organized resistance to desegregation explicitly promoted private alternatives to integrated public schools.

Many of these private academies were explicitly racially exclusive. When the IRS moved in the 1970s to revoke the tax-exempt status of racially discriminatory private schools, the political reaction became one of the organizing forces behind the religious right as a political movement. The public argument shifted from explicit racial exclusion to religious liberty: the freedom of religious schools to operate according to their beliefs. That argument has served as the primary public justification for private schooling ever since, while the racial and economic stratification the system produces has continued largely unchanged.

The connection between private schooling and resistance to integration is not only historical. The private school system as it currently operates, regardless of the founding intentions of any individual school, produces racial and economic stratification that closely mirrors what the explicitly segregationist academies of the post-Brown era produced. The legal framework is different. The outcome is largely the same.

Religious Schools

The most politically complex category of private schools is the religious school. The argument for religious schools rests on two claims: the right of parents to raise their children in their religious tradition, and the right of religious communities to operate educational institutions consistent with their beliefs. Both claims are real. Neither is a sufficient argument for maintaining a separate educational system that produces the segregation and inequality the public school system is constitutionally obligated to address.

The right to raise children in a religious tradition is not the same as the right to educate them in a separate school system supported by public tax exemptions and, increasingly, by public voucher programs. Religious education is available outside school hours, on weekends, and through the existing infrastructure of religious community life. This constitution does not prohibit religious education programs or the formation of religious identity in the home and community. It requires that the publicly supported educational system be a common institution in which all children participate.

A religious school that teaches that certain groups of people are sinful or lesser, that excludes students on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, or that provides a curriculum inconsistent with this constitution's educational obligations, is not simply exercising religious liberty. It is using religious liberty as grounds for reproducing exclusions the constitution prohibits, while benefiting from the tax treatment that makes it financially viable. The resolution is clear: public subsidy is what this constitution controls. Religious institutions may operate educational programs for their communities. They are not entitled to public funding for doing so in ways inconsistent with the constitutional education obligation.

What the Research Says

The argument that private schools produce better educational outcomes than public schools requires careful examination. Studies that appear to show a private school advantage generally do not adequately account for selection effects: the private school student comes from a family with the economic and social resources to choose a private school, to be involved in their child's education, and to provide supplementary support that improves academic outcomes regardless of which school the child attends. When researchers attempt to control for these factors, the private school advantage largely disappears.

The research on school integration is more consistent and more compelling. Students in economically and racially integrated schools show better outcomes, across a wide range of measures, than students in segregated schools. The benefits are not concentrated among lower-income students who gain access to more-resourced schools. They are distributed across the student population. Students from affluent families educated alongside students from less affluent families do not experience a decline in academic outcomes. They gain in the civic capacities that integrated education develops.

The research on civic outcomes is particularly striking. Students educated in socioeconomically diverse settings show greater civic engagement as adults, greater political participation, greater willingness to support public goods, and greater capacity for deliberation across difference. These are capacities that a democracy requires. A student who has never shared a classroom with someone from a different background does not develop them automatically. The private school is not a neutral choice. It has costs for the student who attends it, and for the society that depends on shared civic life.

The Transition

The Timeline

The abolition of private schooling is not instantaneous. The transition requires a timeline long enough to allow families, schools, and communities to adjust, and short enough to constitute a genuine commitment rather than an indefinite deferral. A fifteen-year transition window is appropriate: long enough for the public school system to build the capacity to receive every student, short enough to be a real change rather than a symbolic gesture.

During the transition period, existing private schools continue to operate but receive no new public subsidy: no tax exemptions for new contributions, no voucher funding, no public contracts of any kind. This creates a financial pressure that accelerates the voluntary movement of families and teachers toward the public system as the public system improves. It does not require the immediate closure of any institution.

The Endowments

The endowments of private schools, accumulated over generations through tax-exempt donations, represent a large concentration of educational wealth built with public subsidy. Upon the transition of a private school to public status, or the closure of a private school that does not transition, its endowment transfers to the public school foundation of the jurisdiction in which it operates, to be used for the improvement of public education in that jurisdiction, with priority given to schools serving the lowest-income communities.

Phillips Exeter Academy's endowment is more than one billion dollars for a school of about eleven hundred students. The redirection of that endowment to the public schools of New Hampshire would substantially transform those schools' capacity. The counterargument is that the endowment was donated specifically for private education at Exeter. That is true. It was donated with tax exemptions that represented a public subsidy. The redirection of wealth accumulated through that subsidy toward the public purpose of education is not confiscation. It is the return of what the public made possible to the public that made it possible.

The Teachers

Teachers currently employed in private schools are not responsible for the system they work in and should not bear the cost of the transition. The transition includes full portability of credentials, seniority, and pension rights into the public system for private school teachers who choose to transition. The public system absorbs these teachers with full recognition of their experience.

The transition creates a significant expansion of the public teaching workforce at exactly the moment the public system is being asked to serve a larger and more diverse student population. Private school teachers who transition bring skills, experience, and in many cases specialization in arts, languages, and other subjects the current public system has underinvested in.

Making the Public School Worth Choosing

The abolition of private schooling is only sustainable if the public school system that replaces it is genuinely worth choosing. Families who currently send their children to private schools are not always doing so from a desire to exclude. They are often doing so because the public school available to them does not provide what their child needs: class sizes are too large, course offerings too limited, buildings too deteriorated, safety too uncertain. The transition requires simultaneous investment in the public school system that makes these concerns addressable.

The equalized funding provisions, investment in early childhood education, universal design provisions, curriculum rebuilding, and teacher pay and autonomy provisions described in the education companion document are prerequisites for a public school system that can actually replace what the private system currently provides. The abolition of private schooling without the investment in the public alternative is not a policy. It is a demand. The two must happen together, funded adequately and implemented honestly, for the transition to produce the outcome the philosophy requires.
floor-16-media-and-information:
Media and Information

← Environmental Rights and Obligations · The Floor and the Framework · Security and the Common Defense →

The Commons of Expression and the Right to Know

A Companion Document to the Constitution

The Philosophical Foundation

The media system is the primary mechanism by which shared public reality is produced and maintained. Every day, the decisions made by editors, producers, algorithms, and owners about what is covered and what is not, what is foregrounded and what is buried, whose voice is amplified and whose is filtered out, produce the version of reality that most people receive as simply the news. That production is not neutral. It encodes the interests, the blind spots, and the assumptions of the people making the decisions.

The framework this constitution is built on treats consensus reality as always a political choice. The dominant version of what is happening and why always reflects who is doing the constructing. The question of who controls that construction is the central political question of the information age.

The First Amendment as currently interpreted protects the right to speak. It does not protect the right to be heard, the right to accurate information, or the right to a media ecosystem that represents the full range of human experience rather than the range that is most profitable to represent. The protection of speech without the obligation of infrastructure produces a system in which the speech of people with the most resources drowns out the speech of everyone else, in which platforms optimize for engagement rather than truth, and in which the business model of journalism is the sale of attention to advertisers rather than the provision of accurate information to the public. The result is the media environment we currently inhabit: technically free, substantively captured.

The standard against which the media system must be measured is honest witnessing. A media system that is witnessing honestly does not decide in advance what is worth seeing. It brings the full weight of attention to what is actually there, including what is uncomfortable, including what challenges the dominant version of events, including the interior lives of people whose interior lives the dominant version has decided do not count as newsworthy. The journalism that covers the opioid epidemic as a public health crisis rather than as a criminal justice story is practicing this kind of witnessing. The journalism that covers climate change as an ongoing catastrophe rather than as a dispute between scientists and fossil fuel industry spokespersons is practicing it. Most American journalism is not. It is managing information in ways consistent with the financial interests of its owners.

The Problem of Ownership

The American media system is concentrated in the hands of a small number of corporations whose primary obligation is to their shareholders rather than to the public they ostensibly serve. Six corporations control the majority of American media: the television networks, the film studios, the publishing houses, the news outlets, the streaming platforms. The decisions those corporations make about what to cover, how to cover it, and which voices to amplify are made in the context of the financial interests of the corporation and its advertisers. Coverage that would threaten those interests is systematically underrepresented. Coverage that serves those interests is systematically overrepresented.

The local news crisis is the most acute expression of this concentration. The hedge funds and private equity firms that have purchased local newspapers across the country have applied the same financial logic they apply to any other acquisition: extract the maximum value in the minimum time, cut costs to the bone, and exit before the degradation of the product becomes a financial problem. The result is that thousands of communities have lost the journalism that covered their city council, their school board, their local courts, their local businesses. Communities that have lost local news show measurable declines in civic participation, increases in municipal borrowing costs, and reductions in electoral competition. Local journalism is not a luxury. It is the infrastructure of local democracy.

The consolidation of social media into a small number of companies whose algorithms determine what billions of people see is the newest and most powerful expression of the same problem. The algorithm is not neutral. It is designed to maximize engagement, and engagement is maximized by content that produces strong emotional responses, particularly outrage and fear. The content that produces outrage and fear is often false or misleading. A platform that profits from the spread of false and misleading content has a financial interest in not addressing it. Presenting the algorithm as a neutral technical system rather than a value-laden political choice is exactly the move this constitution's framework is designed to name: a dominant construction presenting itself as natural order.

Independent Public Media

The Constitutional Obligation

This constitution establishes independent public media as a constitutional obligation. Independent means editorially independent from the government that funds it: the model of the BBC, the CBC, and public broadcasters in the Nordic countries, where the funding mechanism insulates editorial decisions from political interference. The government funds the institution; the institution makes its own editorial decisions; neither the government nor any other funder has the power to determine what is covered or how.

Public means serving the full public, not the median consumer, not the demographic most attractive to advertisers, not the audience that already agrees with the editorial perspective. The public broadcaster has an obligation to represent the full range of human experience in this country: the communities that commercial media has decided are not profitable to cover, the stories that challenge the dominant version of events, the voices that are systematically excluded from the commercial media ecosystem. This is an editorial obligation, not a courtesy: the refusal to reproduce the hierarchy that decides which people's lives and experiences count as worth covering.

The funding mechanism must insulate the institution from political pressure. The current public broadcasting system in the United States, PBS and NPR, is funded through a combination of federal appropriations, state appropriations, and private donations, all of which are subject to political pressure. The threat to cut federal funding has been used repeatedly to influence editorial decisions. The alternative is a dedicated funding mechanism, such as a tax on spectrum use by commercial broadcasters or a small fee on digital advertising, that provides stable funding without annual Congressional appropriation and therefore without the leverage that annual appropriation provides.

Plurality as Obligation

The public media system is obligated to represent the full plurality of human voices and experiences, not to reproduce the consensus version of public reality. This means active investment in journalism from and about communities that commercial media systematically undercoverts: rural communities, immigrant communities, indigenous communities, communities of color, disabled communities, communities outside the major metropolitan areas that currently dominate media production. The production of public media from within these communities, not about them from outside, is a practice of honest witnessing: the refusal to treat people who are not the default subject of journalism as background material for someone else's story.

Language access is part of plurality. A country with the linguistic diversity of the United States requires a public media system with substantial production in languages other than English, not as a concession to non-English speakers but as the honest acknowledgment that the full range of public life in this country is not conducted in English. A public media system that only covers the English-speaking public is not covering the full public.

Disinformation and the Limits of Free Speech

This constitution names coordinated disinformation campaigns in referendum contests as election fraud. This document extends that principle and defines its limits. Free speech is the right of every person to express their views without government suppression. It is not the right of any person or institution to deliberately spread false information for the purpose of manipulating democratic processes, suppressing the votes of specific populations, or producing public confusion about matters of documented fact in ways that serve specific financial or political interests.

The distinction between protected speech and election fraud is not a distinction between true and false speech generally. Falsehood is protected speech in most contexts. The distinction is between the organic expression of views, however mistaken, and the coordinated industrial production and distribution of false information for the purpose of corrupting democratic processes. The tobacco industry's decades-long campaign to manufacture doubt about the link between smoking and cancer was not a good-faith expression of scientific disagreement. It was a deliberate fraud. The fossil fuel industry's campaign to manufacture doubt about climate change is the same fraud at larger scale. The political operatives who produce and distribute false information about voting procedures, polling locations, and electoral outcomes are not exercising free speech. They are committing election fraud.

Enforcing this distinction requires an independent regulatory body with genuine authority, adequate resources, and structural independence from the political interests that benefit from the fraud it is charged with preventing. The Federal Election Commission as currently constituted is designed to deadlock: it has six members, three from each party, and cannot act without bipartisan agreement, which is rarely achievable when one party benefits from the disinformation the commission is supposed to prevent. The rebuilt commission has a structure that produces genuine independence from partisan interest, clear authority, and real enforcement capacity.

The Right to Know

Democracy requires an informed public. An informed public requires access to accurate information about what the government is doing and why. The Freedom of Information Act provides some of this access, subject to extensive exemptions and a process slow enough to be functionally inaccessible for most citizens and most journalists working on deadline. The classification system, which removes information from public access on grounds of national security, has been used extensively to conceal information whose primary value to the government is embarrassment prevention rather than genuine security protection.

This constitution's transparency provisions, the real-time disclosure of campaign contributions, the forty-eight-hour disclosure of lobbying contacts, the public availability of officials' financial records, are the demand that power be seen. The right to know is the affirmative corollary of those provisions: not only must the government disclose what the constitution requires, but citizens have a right of access to government information that is enforceable in court, with the burden of proof on the government to demonstrate why disclosure should be denied rather than on the citizen to demonstrate why it should be provided.

The classification system is subject to independent judicial review. The national security claim is not self-executing: the government must demonstrate to an independent court that specific information poses a specific genuine security risk if disclosed. The blanket classification of entire categories of information, the reclassification of information already in the public record, and the classification of information about government programs that are themselves constitutionally questionable are prohibited. The government that classifies information to avoid accountability for its own conduct is using secrecy as a tool of self-protection rather than national protection.

Digital Rights and Platform Accountability

The major digital platforms, the companies that control the infrastructure through which most public communication now occurs, occupy a position with no precedent in the history of communication. They are private companies with no First Amendment obligations. They are also the effective public square: the place where political discourse, civic organization, community formation, and the distribution of news and information primarily happen. The legal framework that treats them as neutral conduits, immune from liability for the content they distribute, was designed for a much earlier version of the internet and does not account for the active role platform algorithms play in determining what content is amplified and what is suppressed.

The privacy provision of this constitution, the requirement that no government or corporation collect personal data without informed revocable consent, is the starting point. The surveillance capitalism model, in which the product being sold is the user's attention and the raw material is the user's personal data, is a constitutional violation under that provision. The person whose browsing history, location data, social connections, purchasing patterns, and political views are collected, aggregated, and sold to advertisers has not genuinely consented simply because they clicked through a terms of service agreement. Long-form terms of service that no one reads and that cannot be declined without losing access to the service are not consent. They are the managed appearance of consent in a system the user has no meaningful power to decline.

Platform accountability for algorithmic amplification of harmful content requires a regulatory framework that can keep pace with technological change: not specific rules about specific content, which are always behind the current form of the harm, but principles and obligations that apply regardless of the specific technology. The platform that profits from the amplification of content that suppresses votes, produces political violence, or spreads demonstrably false information about public health has a legal obligation to the public that its private legal status does not extinguish. The framework for enforcing that obligation is developed through the democratic process, subject to the First Amendment protections that apply to genuine speech, and administered by an independent regulatory body with the technical expertise to understand what it is regulating.

The Transition

The media transition is already happening, badly: the collapse of commercial journalism, the rise of platform-mediated information distribution, the fragmentation of the shared information environment. What is needed is not the preservation of the current system but the deliberate construction of its replacement, built on the principles this document establishes rather than on the financial logic that produced the current crisis.

The investment in public media, in local journalism infrastructure, in digital platforms that serve the public interest rather than the advertising market, in the media literacy education that gives people the tools to navigate the information environment they actually inhabit: these are not narrow media policy questions. They are the prerequisites for the democracy this constitution requires. The people cannot be the government if they cannot know what the government is doing. The people cannot make informed decisions about the laws that govern them if the information environment has been optimized for engagement rather than truth. The floor of the information commons is the floor of democracy itself.
floor-09-the-economic-system:
The Economic System

← The Abolition of Private Schooling · The Floor and the Framework · Voting and Electoral Systems →

What the Economy Is For and How to Build One That Serves Everyone

A Companion Document to the Constitution

The Philosophical Foundation

Capitalism presents itself as the natural expression of human nature. People are self-interested. Markets aggregate those interests efficiently. The outcomes are therefore the natural result of who people are and what they deserve. This is the most consequential construction of the second pillar: an economic system built at a specific historical moment by specific people with specific interests, producing specific outcomes that serve those interests, presenting itself as the inevitable expression of human nature and economic law. It is not. It is a choice. It was built. It can be rebuilt.

The assumptions underneath the construction are worth naming. Human beings are primarily self-interested individuals rather than relational, communal, plural selves: this is the first pillar's singular acceptable self applied to economic theory. Value is what the market will pay rather than what sustains life and enables flourishing: this is the second pillar's consensus reality applied to the accounting of what matters. The care economy, the work of raising children and tending the sick and maintaining the relationships on which all other economic activity depends, is not counted because the market does not pay for it: this is the third pillar's permanent grief, the accumulated loss of the work that sustains everything and is recognized by nothing.

The economic floor, which the constitution establishes as a right that can be enforced in court, is not charity. It is the philosophical prerequisite for everything else in the document. The person whose entire cognitive and emotional bandwidth is consumed by not having enough to eat or nowhere to sleep cannot develop the plural self, cannot grieve honestly, cannot witness, cannot build recursively. Research on trauma and the nervous system is clear: a person in survival mode cannot access the psychological bandwidth needed to act from their values, reflect on who they are, or build toward a different future. The floor is not a supplement to the philosophy. It is the material condition without which the philosophy cannot be lived.

What the Current System Is Actually Doing

The Distribution of Wealth and Power

The United States has among the highest levels of wealth inequality of any wealthy democracy. The top one percent of households holds nearly as much wealth as the bottom ninety percent combined. This concentration has increased consistently over the past fifty years, accelerating since the 2008 financial crisis and the COVID-19 pandemic. The Gini coefficient, a numerical scale economists use to measure how unequally income is distributed across a population, has increased consistently since the 1970s and is now higher than at any point since the Great Depression.

This concentration of wealth is not the outcome of a neutral market that rewards superior contribution. It is the outcome of a series of deliberate policy choices: the reduction of top marginal tax rates, the deregulation of financial markets, the weakening of labor law and union rights, the treatment of capital income more favorably than labor income, the provision of public subsidies to industries that then used their profits to further influence the policies affecting them. Each of these choices was made by people with the political power to make them, for the benefit of people with the economic power to fund the political power that made them. The construction is self-reinforcing. Concentrated wealth produces concentrated political power which produces policies that further concentrate wealth.

The political consequences of wealth concentration are documented. A landmark study by political scientists Martin Gilens and Benjamin Page examined twenty years of policy outcomes and found that the preferences of economic elites and organized business interests have a substantial independent impact on policy, while average citizens and mass-based interest groups have little or no independent influence. In plain terms: the policies this country adopts reflect what wealthy people and corporations want, not what most people want. The democratic system described by the constitution, in which the people are the government, does not exist in the presence of the level of wealth concentration the current economic system produces. The economic system and the democratic system are in fundamental conflict. One of them has to change.

The Poverty Trap

The American poverty trap is the most thoroughly documented feature of the economic system and the most thoroughly ignored in the design of the policies that claim to address it. The poor are poor not because they have failed to make the choices that would lift them out of poverty but because the system is designed to keep them in it. The loss of benefits at income thresholds that make marginal increases in income economically irrational. The cost of childcare that exceeds the income from the job that would pay for it. The lack of transportation that makes the job inaccessible. The criminal record from the drug conviction that forecloses the employment that would have provided the income. The medical debt from the untreated condition that became an emergency that became a bankruptcy. Each of these is a deliberate feature of the system, not an accidental outcome of neutral market forces.

The poverty trap is the political system demanding performed recovery from conditions the political system produced. The person in the poverty trap is not failing to lift themselves up by their bootstraps. They are carrying the accumulated weight of a system designed to keep specific people in specific positions, performing the agency the system denies them. The economic floor is not the complete solution to the poverty trap. It is the condition without which no solution is possible: the assurance that survival does not depend on the perfect navigation of a system designed to produce failure.

The Solidarity Economy

Worker Ownership and Cooperatives

The worker cooperative is the oldest and most thoroughly researched alternative to the conventional firm. In a worker cooperative, the people who work in the enterprise own and govern it. Decisions about wages, working conditions, investment, and strategy are made democratically by the worker-owners rather than by a separate class of capital owners or their hired managers. The profits, rather than flowing primarily to the capital owners, are distributed among the worker-owners or retained for investment in the enterprise.

The Mondragon Corporation in the Basque Country of Spain is the most studied large-scale example: a network of worker cooperatives employing over eighty thousand people across manufacturing, retail, education, and finance, with sixty years of evidence on its economic performance and its effects on the communities it operates in. The Mondragon cooperatives have consistently outperformed conventional firms in their sectors on the measure of employment stability: during economic downturns, cooperatives reduce hours and wages before they reduce employment, distributing the pain of the downturn across all worker-owners rather than concentrating it on the workers with the least power. The result is communities that are more economically resilient and more equal than communities organized around conventional firms.

The public investment in worker ownership includes the cooperative development infrastructure: the technical assistance, the financing mechanisms, the legal frameworks that make it possible for workers to purchase the enterprises that employ them when owners retire or businesses are sold. The conversion of conventional businesses to worker ownership at the moment of sale, rather than the sale to private equity that extracts value and then discards the workforce, is one of the most consequential economic policy choices available and one of the least politically contested. The owners get their market price. The workers get ownership. The community keeps the enterprise.

Community Land Trusts

The community land trust removes land from the speculative market and holds it in permanent affordability. The trust owns the land and leases it to the people who use it, whether for housing or for commercial purposes, at prices that reflect the actual cost of the use rather than the speculative value of the land. The buildings and improvements on the land can be bought and sold, but the land itself remains in the trust in perpetuity, and the sale price of the buildings is limited to prevent the speculative appreciation that makes housing progressively unaffordable.

Community land trusts have been operating in the United States since the 1960s and the research on their outcomes is consistent: they produce housing that remains affordable across generations rather than affordable only until the market appreciates it away, they build community wealth rather than transferring it to landlords and speculators, and they provide housing security to people for whom market-rate housing is permanently inaccessible. The Champlain Housing Trust in Burlington, Vermont, is one of the largest and most studied examples: forty years of evidence on the production and preservation of permanently affordable housing in a market that would otherwise have displaced the people it serves.

The scaling of community land trusts requires public investment in land acquisition: the use of public resources to remove land from the speculative market and place it in permanent community ownership. This is a direct application of the economic floor to the housing provision of Article VII: the assurance that the floor of housing security does not depend on the behavior of a market that is organized around the extraction of maximum rent from people who need shelter.

Public Banking

The Bank of North Dakota is the only publicly owned state bank in the United States and it has operated since 1919. It partners with local banks rather than competing with them, providing the capital and the backing that allows local banks to make loans that the national banks would not make. It has been consistently profitable, including during the 2008 financial crisis when many private banks required public bailouts. Its profits return to the state government rather than to private shareholders.

Public banking at the federal level means a public option for banking services: the person who cannot meet the minimum balance requirements of a private bank, who is therefore unbanked or subject to the predatory fees of check cashing services, has access to basic banking services through the public system. It means the availability of credit to communities and enterprises that the private banking system has decided are not profitable enough to serve. It means the retention of the profits from banking within the public system rather than their extraction to private shareholders. The Federal Reserve already performs many of these functions at the monetary policy level. The public bank extends them to the retail banking level where most people actually interact with the financial system.

The Care Economy

The care economy is the work of raising children, tending the sick and elderly, maintaining households, and sustaining the relationships on which all other economic activity depends. It is performed primarily by women. It is largely unpaid or poorly paid. It is not counted in GDP. It is the foundation on which the market economy rests and the thing the market economy most systematically refuses to recognize.

Economists working in the feminist tradition have developed rigorous methods for counting care work in economic accounting. Studies tracking what it would cost to replace unpaid household and care work at market rates estimate that this work represents between twenty and thirty percent of GDP. The economic system that does not count this work has decided in advance that the work of women does not count as economic activity. That decision is reversed here.

The counting of care work is not only a measurement change. It is the foundation for the policy changes that follow: the recognition that care workers deserve pay and benefits and protections commensurate with the economic value of the work they perform, the investment in care infrastructure that makes the care economy more productive and less dependent on the unpaid and undervalued labor of women, the design of the work system around the full range of human needs rather than around the needs of the worker who has no care responsibilities because someone else is performing them invisibly.

Paid family and medical leave, universal childcare, elder care as a public responsibility rather than a private burden: these are not benefits. They are the infrastructure of the care economy, the investment that makes the rest of the economy possible. The country that does not provide paid parental leave, as the United States uniquely does not among wealthy democracies, is not a country that values families. It is a country that has decided that the cost of care should be externalized onto the people performing it rather than shared by the economy that benefits from it.

Taxation and the Floor

What Taxation Is For

Taxation is the mechanism by which the collective funds the collective's obligations. It is not punishment for success. It is the return of a portion of what was made possible by the collective infrastructure: the educated workforce, the legal system, the public research, the stable currency, the transportation network, the public health system, the physical security, the accumulated social capital of the community in which the economic activity occurred. The person who has accumulated great wealth did so in the context of all of these public goods. The taxation of that wealth to fund the continuation of those goods is not redistribution. It is the return of what the commons made possible to the commons that made it possible.

The Current System's Inversions

The current tax system taxes income from labor more heavily than income from capital. The person who earns their income by working pays a higher marginal rate than the person whose income comes from investments that appreciate while they sleep. This is a political choice, not an economic law. It reflects the interests of the people who have accumulated enough capital that their income comes primarily from capital rather than labor, and the political power they have used to write a tax code that serves those interests.

Consider three specific mechanisms through which the wealthiest avoid taxation at the rates the rest of us pay. The carried interest loophole allows private equity managers to pay tax on their earnings at the lower investment rate rather than the higher rate that applies to regular income, even though the money is compensation for their work. The stepped-up basis rule means that when someone inherits assets, the tax on any increase in value accumulated over the original owner's lifetime is wiped out entirely: enormous wealth passes between generations without the taxation that would otherwise apply. And transfer pricing allows large corporations to manipulate their internal accounting to make profits appear in low-tax countries while keeping costs in high-tax ones, shifting the tax burden off corporations and onto everyone else. Each of these is a political choice presented as neutral tax planning. Each costs the public treasury billions of dollars per year.

What the System Requires

Progressive taxation of income, with top marginal rates adequate to fund the floor and the public goods the constitution establishes. The research on the economic effects of top marginal rates does not support the claim that higher rates produce lower economic growth: the postwar decades of American prosperity, the period of the greatest expansion of the middle class and the greatest reduction of inequality, were decades of top marginal rates above ninety percent. The claim that high marginal rates destroy economic activity is the defense of the dominant construction: the interests of the people who benefit from low top rates presented as universal economic law.

Taxation of wealth as well as income. An annual wealth tax on assets above a defined threshold, graduated to increase with the level of wealth, produces revenue and reduces the concentration that makes the democratic system impossible. Economists Emmanuel Saez and Gabriel Zucman, who have spent their careers documenting the scale of wealth concentration and designing policy responses to it, have demonstrated both the feasibility and the revenue potential of a wealth tax at the scale needed to fund the floor.

The closure of the loopholes, havens, and mechanisms that enable the largest accumulations of wealth to pay the lowest effective tax rates. The implementation of a global minimum corporate tax, which has been agreed in principle by most wealthy countries, that prevents the competitive lowering of corporate tax rates that has shifted the burden from capital to labor over the past decades. The taxation of financial transactions at a small rate that does not affect the long-term investor but significantly affects high-frequency trading that extracts value from markets without contributing to their function.

Measuring What Matters

GDP measures the total value of goods and services produced in the economy. It does not measure whether the people in the economy are healthy, educated, housed, safe, or able to live full lives. It counts the economic activity produced by the car accident alongside the economic activity produced by the medical care that follows. It counts the cost of cleaning up the oil spill. It does not subtract the cost of the environmental damage the spill produced. It counts the production of weapons. It does not count the care work that sustains the workers who produce everything else.

Economist Kate Raworth's doughnut economics framework provides a different accounting: the economy is doing well when it operates within the social foundation, the floor of human needs represented by the rights in Article VII, and within the ecological ceiling, the planetary boundaries within which human civilization can sustain itself. The space between the floor and the ceiling is the space where human life can be lived. Growth that pushes through the ecological ceiling or that leaves people below the social foundation is not success. It is failure, regardless of what the GDP figure shows.

Several alternative economic measures attempt to track what the economy is actually producing in terms of human flourishing rather than the market value of activity. None of them is perfect. All of them are more honest than GDP as a measure of whether the economy is doing what the economy is supposed to do. The adoption of a comprehensive wellbeing measure alongside GDP as the official measure of national economic performance is the second pillar applied to accounting: the refusal to let the dominant construction of what counts as economic success continue to present itself as the objective measure of how things are going.

The Transition

The transition from the current economic system to the one this document describes is the longest and most politically contested of all the transitions the companion documents require. The current system is deeply embedded and resistant to change, defended by people with enormous resources to deploy in its defense, and embedded in international legal frameworks, trade agreements, and financial architectures that would need to be renegotiated.

The transition is not instantaneous and does not require the simultaneous transformation of every element of the current system. It requires a direction and the consistent movement of policy in that direction. The direction is toward an economy that starts from the floor rather than the market price, that counts the care economy, that treats the natural world as a rights-holder rather than a resource, that measures wellbeing rather than growth, that is organized around the plural self rather than the singular productive unit, that builds the commons rather than extracting from it.

Every policy choice that moves in that direction is part of the building. Every cooperative formed, every community land trust established, every public bank opened, every care worker whose work is recognized and compensated, every loophole closed, every wellbeing measure adopted alongside GDP: these are the building that knows it is building. The map that knows it is wrong before the ink dries and draws itself anyway. The fifth pillar enacted as economic policy.

The floor, once established, is not retracted. The commons, once built, belongs to everyone.

Voting and Electoral Systems
